1.1   A.1. The integral quotient and its three-dimensional target

                                                2
The formula
                                 [z, Π(z)x] 7−→ ([z], γ(x) mod Z)                            (A.1.1)
defines a real-analytic fibrewise group epimorphism J −→ B ◦ × S 1 with connected kernel TL .
At the finite fillings it descends to a smooth proper T 3 -bundle over a Seifert solid torus, of
multiplicities 3 and 4 and translation residues 1 and −1.

Proof. The first two displayed matrices are the inverse transposes of the matrices printed
on page 2 of [CA26]; their product has inverse M0 . Direct integral multiplication gives
A31 = A42 = A1 A2 M0 = I and Aj vj = vj . Solving the two fixed-vector equations gives
(0, 0, 0, d0 ). For a row vector (a, b, c, e), the first fixed-covector equation gives b = 2c, e = 3c
and the second gives b = c, e = 2c; therefore b = c = e = 0. Also

                      (M0 − I)(a, b, c, e) = (0, 0, b, −a),       A1 w = u − w.

These identities prove the assertions about L and the cusp lattice K = Zhw, di. Their
primitivity follows from the displayed bases. The flat real marking identifies the deck action
on a fibre with x 7→ Aj x. Since γAj = γ, (A.1.1) descends. Its kernel is connected because γ
is primitive.
    On a root disc the affine generator is

                (s, x) 7−→ (e−2πi/m s, Aj x + vj /m),         (m, κ) = (3, 1), (4, −1).

It induces (s, θ) 7→ (e−2πi/m s, θ + κ/m) on the character quotient. This action is free since
gcd(κ, m) = 1. Writing a = e2πiθ and choosing r with rκ ≡ 1 (mod m), the invariant
coordinates sar and am identify its quotient with D2 × S 1 . The base coordinate becomes
(sar )m (am )−r , and hence has multiplicity m at its central circle. Before the finite quotient
the map is a trivial TL -bundle. The free actions on source and target are equivariant for that
map, so it descends locally to a smooth TL -bundle. Properness follows from compactness of
TL . The logarithmic translation used to glue the root chart to J changes the character by its
γ-component. Applying γ to the actual gluing translation therefore gives the target gluing,
proving agreement on every overlap. The exact checks, including the exhaustive mod-two
fixed-vector calculation used below, are in code/maps_exact.py.

   Engel’s primitive invariant covector is named ψ in his Lemma 3.8, labelled covect in the
supplied source [Eng26a]. It is not named ε there. In his common marking B0 , the integral
comparison is                                   

sign convention in the supplied family return, B.2.2; it explains why equality of the unnamed

Proposition A.1.2 (Refuted as stated; corrected). The literal character has no
continuous extension at either triple point or at generic points of two of the three double
curves. It has the constant limit 0 on the smooth locus of W and on the third double curve
away from the triple points. In the chart q = z0 z1 z2 , x1 = z1 , x2 = z2 , the extendible double
curve is z0 = z1 = 0, z2 6= 0. The fixed curve of the C∗ -action in direction d = e2 is instead
z0 = z2 = 0, z1 6= 0, and is one of the nonextendible curves. Consequently the parenthesis in
A.1 identifying the extendible curve with the fixed curve is false.

The choices a = (−1/4, 1/4) and a0 = (−1/2, 1/4) have logarithmic positions tending to
(1/4, 1/4) and (1/4, 1/2). Both are interior to the triangle with vertices 0, e1 , e2 , so all three

at the first triple point. The other triangle type has vertices e1 , e2 , e1 + e2 . Its coordinates
can be taken as x1 x2 /q, q/x2 , q/x1 . Positions (3/4, 3/4) and (3/4, 1/2) lie in its interior, give
distinct values of −y2 modulo one, and converge to its origin. Translation by the lattice
preserves triangle type; these are precisely the two triple points of W .
    For arbitrary convergent paths in the first chart, inversion of the exact logarithmic period
matrix gives
                                         log |z2 |
                                 θγ = −            + o(1) (mod Z).                           (A.1.4)

Here the error tends to zero whenever the logarithmic ratios stay bounded; they do stay
bounded near a fixed point of a normal-crossing stratum because q = z0 z1 z2 and the three
coordinates are bounded. If z0 , z1 → 0 and z2 → c 6= 0, the right side tends to zero. If
z0 , z2 → 0 and z1 = c 6= 0, the paths z2 = q a , z0 = q 1−a /c, 0 < a < 1, have limits −a
(mod 1) at the same double point. The same construction with z0 = c proves nonextension
on z1 = z2 = 0. At a smooth point of a component the ratio in (A.1.4) tends to 0 or 1, giving
zero modulo one. Integer translates of these charts give the stated assertion on all of W .
     The torus action in direction e2 = d is

                                 λ · (z0 , z1 , z2 ) = (λ−1 z0 , z1 , λz2 ).

Its fixed curve is z0 = z2 = 0. This directly locates the incorrect identification in the
prompt. Edge direction, torus stabilizer, and coordinate on the quotient polygon must not
be interchanged.

   The nonextension above is local and pointwise. It does not contradict extension of the
cohomology class over a cusp neighbourhood. The toric covering has rays (v, 1) for all
v ∈ Z2 . Meridians about its toric divisors kill the whole cocharacter lattice: (0, 1) is a ray
and (ei , 1) − (0, 1) = (ei , 0). The toric cover is therefore simply connected. Its free period
deck group is Λ and hence
                                        π1 (N0 ) = Λ = Λ/K.                               (A.1.5)
For the punctured cusp the map to this group kills K and the base meridian. The latter
bounds the disc given by a point of the dense orbit on a central component. Both long-period
covectors extend in integral H 1 , since they kill precisely these relations. In contrast, an
extension of θγ to all of X ≃ S 6 would induce a nonzero map H1 (F ) → Z factoring through
H1 (X) = 0, which is impossible. This last argument is the global cohomological obstruction
K5; it says nothing about pointwise cusp limits.

Proposition A.1.3 (Proved). For the original data the quotient over the complement of
the cusp disc is the exterior of the (3, 4) torus knot, with the specified Seifert structure. For
general admissible (l0 , l1 , l2 ) the filled quotient is the lens space determined by the following
meridian slopes in one oriented integral torus basis (ρ1 , h):

      µ1 = (3, −l1 ),    µ2 = (−4, 4l0 − l2 ),             det(µ1 , µ2 ) = p = 12l0 − 4l1 − 3l2 .   (A.1.6)

In the lens-space convention that the second meridian is −q0 µ1 + pλ1 , where det(µ1 , λ1 ) = 1,
the lens parameter satisfies 3q0 ≡ 4 (mod p). In particular the target depends only on the
signed integer p, and is a three-sphere exactly when |p| = 1.

Proof. Let P be the three-holed sphere, with oriented boundary meridians ρ0 + ρ1 + ρ2 = 0
and positive fibre h. The two finite meridian relations are 3ρ1 − l1 h = 0 and 4ρ2 − l2 h = 0;
the cusp solid-torus meridian is ρ0 + l0 h. Eliminating ρ0 gives ρ2 = l0 h − ρ1 on the annulus
joining the finite solid tori, which gives exactly (A.1.6). Since both slopes are primitive, this
is a genus-one Heegaard splitting. Choose a, b ∈ Z with al1 + 3b = 1 and put λ1 = (a, b).
Direct multiplication gives

                    µ2 = −q0 µ1 + pλ1 ,      q0 = a(4l0 − l2 ) + 4b,       3q0 − ap = 4.            (A.1.7)

This proves the claimed lens parameter in a convention fixed by actual meridians, including
orientations. The fundamental group of this gluing is Z/|p|. Admissibility implies gcd(p, 6) =
1, so the modular inverse of 3 used above exists.
    For (l0 , l1 , l2 ) = (0, 1, −1) the two exceptional-fibre data are (3, 1), (4, −1). They are
realized by the circle action

                            s · (z1 , z2 ) = (e4is z1 , e3is z2 )   on S 3 ⊂ C2 .

Its invariant map is [z13 : z24 ]; the local circle translation residues are 4−1 = 1 (mod 3) and
3−1 = −1 (mod 4). Removing a regular orbit gives the same two Seifert solid tori and their
product annulus as above. A regular orbit is the (3, 4) torus knot, up to the harmless exchange
of the two coordinates. This identifies the manifold with its peripheral structure; the abstract
presentation hx, y | x3 = y −4 i alone would not have justified that identification.

1.2     A.2. The repaired map and the scope of its uniqueness
Theorem A.2.1 (Proved). For every admissible member, there is a smooth map e : X → Q
over B whose restriction outside an arbitrarily small cusp neighbourhood is the literal circle
quotient. For fixed quotient gluing, its homotopy class is independent of the cusp replacement,
provided the replacement maps the cusp neighbourhood into its designated solid torus and
is kept fixed on its outer collar. In particular there is a well-defined class for the original
member X ≃ S 6 .

Proof. On the cusp boundary use the product coordinates (q, θγ ) after the specified collar
shear. By (A.1.5), the boundary circle class extends to N0 . Since S 1 = K(Z, 1), it has a
continuous representative θ0 : N0 → S 1 . Its restriction to the boundary is homotopic to the
given one: the two maps induce the same homomorphism on π1 of the boundary mapping
torus. The homotopy-extension property for a manifold with boundary changes θ0 on a
collar so that it agrees exactly with θγ there. Relative smooth approximation gives a smooth
representative, still equal on a smaller collar. Then (f, θ0 ) is the required map into D2 × S 1 ,
and agrees with the finite-filling maps on the overlap. This proves smoothness even at the
critical points of f : the product map is smooth without any submersion assertion.


                                                       5
    The inclusion ∂N0 → N0 surjects on π1 , as (A.1.5) explicitly shows. It follows that
H 1 (N0 ; Z) → H 1 (∂N0 ; Z) is injective. Since both spaces are connected, the long exact
sequence gives H 1 (N0 , ∂N0 ; Z) = 0. Two circle replacements agreeing on the boundary
therefore have quotient whose relative H 1 class is zero, hence have a relative homotopy.
Keeping the base coordinate fixed gives the required homotopy of maps into the solid torus.
Different choices of the collar size are compared on a common smaller collar. This proves the
assertion.

Proposition A.2.2 (Refuted as an unrestricted uniqueness assertion). Agreement
with the literal quotient outside a neighbourhood of W , without a condition on the image of
that neighbourhood, does not determine a homotopy class S 6 → S 3 . All twelve classes occur
among maps satisfying that bare agreement condition.

Proof. Take a closed embedded six-ball in the interior of the cusp neighbourhood. Homotope
a given extension on a smaller ball to be constant there, keeping its boundary and the
complement fixed; a target coordinate ball around the image of its centre provides the
contraction. Pinch the smaller ball to S 6 ∨ D6 relative to its boundary and insert any based
map α : S 6 → S 3 on the new sphere. The resulting global map agrees with the original map
off that ball, and represents [e] + α under [S 6 , S 3 ] = π6 (S 3 ). Distinct α give distinct classes.
Smooth relative approximation preserves this conclusion. The insertion cannot be performed
within the cusp solid torus, since that solid torus has π6 = 0; this is exactly the distinction in
Theorem A.2.1.

   The corrected content of [Eng26a, Remark 8.3] is therefore a quotient over the regular
part and the two finite fillings, followed by a replacement within its circle homotopy class
over a cusp collar. The literal character does not extend. The replacement gives a canonical
homotopy class when the solid-torus image condition is retained.

1.3   A.3. The two real forms and their fixed sets
In this subsection d = δb and g = γ b. We write D1 , D2 , D12 for the three cusp double curves
belonging to edges in directions e1 , e2 , e1 − e2 , respectively. Thus D2 is the fixed sphere of
the circle action ρ, whereas D1 is the double curve along which the literal character has a
limit. This distinction is essential in the real calculation as well.

Proposition A.3.1 (Proved; Lead 9). For a real member the antiholomorphic involutions
have exactly two conjugacy classes under holomorphic automorphisms. For any fixed involutive
splitting σ they are represented by σ and ρ(1/2)σ. Every nonempty fixed set is a closed
connected orientable totally real three-manifold with the mod-two homology of S 3 . The circle
ρ preserves each such fixed set and acts semifreely on it.

Proof. The checked real comparison has derivative complex conjugation in the second
period coordinate. It therefore conjugates translation by b ∈ C/Z to translation by b̄.
In multiplicative notation its action is z 7→ 1/z̄. The square of zσ is z/z̄, so it is an involution
exactly for z ∈ R∗ . Conjugation by y ∈ C∗ changes this coefficient to |y|2 z, giving exactly
its two signs. The automorphism computation used here is the supplied family return B.4.1:
the integral centralizer has linear part aI, the cusp and finite norm equations force a = 1 for
a self-map, and the global translation sheaf has H 0 = Cd with integral periods Zd. These
are precisely the three steps needed to identify the full group with C∗ , rather than only its
identity component.



                                                  6
    At a fixed point an antiholomorphic involution has a real three-dimensional fixed tangent
space, and its complexification is the full tangent space. An invariant metric and its
exponential map identify its fixed locus locally with this real subspace. It is therefore a
closed totally real three-manifold. Smith’s theorem, in the form of [Knu04, Theorem 4.1(1)],
applies to the smooth finite action on the sphere and gives the stated mod-two homology.
A nonempty three-dimensional fixed set is consequently connected, and its first mod-two
cohomology vanishes; its orientation class w1 therefore vanishes. On the unit circle 1/z̄ = z,
so σ commutes with ρ. Its stabilizers are inherited from the checked semifree action on X
and hence are either trivial or the whole circle.

   We now fix a representative of each sign class, instead of leaving the symbol σ unspecified.

    For completeness, the finite arithmetic deciding existence can be performed without
approximating the periods. An affine involution x 7→ R• x + β has a fixed point if and only if
its square translation (I + R• )β belongs to (I + R• )Λ. In (A.3.2) the square translation is

For c = 1/2 + iy the values 2<S on the three arcs are −1/3, −4/3, −2/3; for c = −1/2 + iy
they are 1/2, 0, 0. The resulting integral square vectors are respectively (2w, 0, 2w) and
(3w, d, 3w). Adding d/2 to the involution adds d to each square vector. Taking column
Hermite normal forms of I + R• gives exactly the nonempty entries in the table. All three
I − R• have nonzero Smith factors 1, 2. This proves the coset counts and offsets; the complete
exact computation is in code/real_involutions.py. In particular the lift on the left arc is
g0−1 , not g0 ; the latter would give a nonintegral square vector and is the wrong continuation
convention.
    At t = 0 the root degree is odd. Conjugation by the degree-three deck group acts
transitively on the three reflection lifts; the centralizer of a reflection in that deck group is


                                                8
trivial. Thus the quotient has exactly the same two real tori as the adjacent nonempty real
regular fibres. In the empty cases there are none. This also follows by solving the limiting
affine equations, and checks the full multiplicity-three quotient rather than treating it as a
reduced unramified fibre.
    At t = 1 write the affine deck map as G(x) = A2 x + v2 /4. The real root involution has
matrix R> and translation

                       b− = (1/3, 0, 0, −1/6)t ,       b+ = (1/2, 0, 0, 1/4)t

for the two parameter signs. The real locus of the quotient is the quotient of the fixed sets
of Gk h, 0 ≤ k < 4. Its even and odd lift parities are identified internally by G, while G2
preserves each parity. Direct integer congruences show that the nonempty lift parities are:
both for negative w and  = 0; only even for negative w and  = 1; neither for positive w
and  = 0; only odd for positive w and  = 1. Every nonempty lift has two tori, exchanged
by G2 . Each parity therefore contributes one torus downstairs, not a Klein bottle. The
exhaustive congruence check code/real_finite_four.py uses denominator 24: translation
denominators divide 12, and the nonzero Smith factors are 1, 2, so every component has such
a representative. It checks the component permutation, not just the dimension of the fixed
eigenspace. The normal real line has fourth power of sign positive for the even parity and
negative for the odd parity. This establishes the two one-sided endpoints at t = 1 recorded in
the table.

a singular fibre. Put A = C12 (0); the cusp normalization gives

Theorem A.3.3 (Proved; the real three-manifolds). Every nonempty fixed set in
Theorem A.3.2 is diffeomorphic to S 3 . Its fundamental group is trivial and its integral
homology is (Z, 0, 0, Z). For negative imaginary w, the restricted circle action is the standard

                                                   9
semifree action on S 3 with fixed circle D2σc . For positive imaginary w, the nonempty real
form has a free circle action isomorphic, up to circle and orientation conventions, to the Hopf
action.

Proof. For negative imaginary w both fixed manifolds meet D2 in one circle. Their circle
action is semifree, so the orbit space is a compact orientable surface with boundary. The
local quotient at a fixed circle is the quotient of S 1 × C by scalar rotation on C, hence is
a boundary collar. Over the surface interior the principal circle bundle is trivial because
the surface has boundary and H 2 = 0. Changes of boundary trivialization extend over the
attached normal discs by rotation. Thus the three-manifold is

                                (B × S 1 ) ∪∂B×S 1 (∂B × D2 ).

If B has genus gB and bB boundary components, van Kampen or its surface handle
decomposition gives first homology Z2gB +bB −1 . Smith’s theorem makes this rank zero.
Since bB > 0, we have gB = 0, bB = 1. The displayed manifold is then ∂(D2 × D2 ) = S 3 ,
with the indicated circle action. This derives the smooth recognition from an explicit surface
decomposition.
    For positive imaginary w the nonempty real manifold is free under ρ. The two real tori
on t < 1 join at the single real torus over 1. At 0 the odd root comparison is a torus product.
At infinity they are capped by the real neighbourhoods of D1 and D12 . These are solid tori:
the primitive circle in the edge direction collapses and the remaining real circle is their core.
In the outer real-fibre lattice Zhw, di the two cap meridians are w and w − d.
    We check the intervening torus identification. Put B1 = A−12 A1 A2 and C = B1 . The two
                                                                    −1               2

real-arc involutions satisfy R< Rm = B1 , Rm B1 Rm = B1 and B1 = I. Moving between the
                                                          −1        3

real root lifts requires B1k Rm B1−k = B1 Rm , so 2k ≡ 1 (mod 3) and k = 2. Thus the actual
odd-root transport is C, not merely an arbitrary matrix conjugating the two reflections. It
satisfies R< = CRm C −1 , and C(u + w) = −w + d. The exchange across the multiplicity-four
real torus is A22 ; after this odd-root transport it is CA22 C −1 , whose restriction to hw, di
is w 7→ −w, d 7→ d. Consequently the meridians, compared on one boundary torus, have
determinant of absolute value one. The resulting genus-one Heegaard splitting is S 3 : primitive
meridians intersecting once can be taken to the two coordinate circles by an integral torus
automorphism, giving the usual two solid tori of S 3 . The free circle d then has Euler number
of absolute value one, so the displayed bundle over S 2 is the Hopf bundle. This proves the
integral assertions, beyond the mod-two information.

2     B. Homotopy classes and parameter monodromy
2.1   B.1. The framed three-torus and the class of e
We use π3S = Z/24hνi, with eR (ν) = 1/24, and π6 (S 3 ) = Z/12hν 0 i, where the stabilization of
ν 0 is 2ν. We write ηn : S n+1 → S n for the (n − 2)-fold suspension of the complex Hopf map.
The order-two classes below are unaffected by reversal of either source or target orientation.
An orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the standard sphere transports its bounding
stable framing to T X ⊕ R. Its homotopy class does not depend on that diffeomorphism: two
oriented stable trivializations differ by a map S 6 → SO, and π6 (SO) = 0 by [Bot59, Corollary
to Theorem II and the table on p. 315]. We use outward stabilization and the convention
that the normal frame precedes the tangential frame; a constant permutation is corrected
once to preserve orientation.

Lemma B.1.1 (Proved). Let F be a regular fibre of the original fibration. Compare the
ambient stable framing of the oriented sphere X with the framing on T X|F consisting of four
translation-invariant vertical vector fields and an oriented lifted base frame. The restriction
of their stable difference to any coset of TL ⊂ F is null-homotopic.

Proof. After a constant orientation adjustment the comparison is a map D : F → SO, where
stabilization is understood. Its homotopy class is invariant under both monodromies. Indeed,
transport F around a based loop in B ◦ using the flat real marking. The translated vertical
frame varies continuously on F × [0, 1]; at the endpoint it changes by the constant real matrix
of the affine monodromy. An oriented base frame can be chosen periodic along the loop.
The space of lifts of that frame to T X is affine, so changing the lift does not affect the
comparison class. The ambient stable framing is already defined along this entire cylinder.
Thus the comparison at its endpoints is D and D ◦ Aj times a constant positive matrix. Every
such constant matrix is path connected to the identity. This proves [D] = A∗j [D]. An affine
translational part is isotopic to the identity and has no effect.
    The map on fundamental groups defines σ(D) ∈ H 1 (F ; Z/2). The exhaustive calculation
in maps_exact.py gives
                               H 1 (F ; Z/2)hA1 ,A2 i = {0, γ mod 2}.
Both classes vanish on L, so D|TL lifts to Spin. Up to dimension four the latter has
π1 = π2 = π4 = 0, π3 = Z. Obstruction theory consequently identifies maps from a
three- or four-dimensional torus to Spin with H 3 of that torus. The two possible lifts differ
by multiplication by the central element −1, which is homotopic to the identity, so this
identification has no unrecorded lifting ambiguity.
   The doubled stable difference 2[D] has zero σ, and therefore corresponds to a monodromy-
invariant class in H 3 (F ; Z). Integral Poincare duality, natural for these determinant-one
monodromies, identifies the invariants in H 3 (F ; Z) with the fixed vectors Zd ⊂ H1 (F ; Z).


                                              11
Such a class evaluates to zero on TL , since d ∈ L: its evaluation is the determinant with
columns d, u, w, d. Hence 2[D|TL ] = 0 in [TL , Spin] = Z. This group has no torsion; thus
[D|TL ] = 0. The same argument applies to a coset since translation is isotopic to the
identity.

Theorem B.2.1 (Proved). The map f : X → P1 of the original sphere construction is
null-homotopic. This conclusion does not require the choice of e.
Proof. The quotient projection h : Q → B is, after the orientation-preserving identifications

its two exceptional values to 0, 1. It is the ordinary Hopf map after the self-map

At a value with both coordinates nonzero, its phase map has 3 · 4 = 12 preimages, all with
positive local degree; its radial coordinate is strictly increasing. Consequently its degree
is twelve. A degree-k map of S 3 is homotopic to the kth power map of the topological
group S 3 . On π6 (S 3 ) the latter is multiplication by k, since pointwise multiplication and the
homotopy-group addition agree. Thus h∗ = (η2 )∗ ◦ 12 = 0 on π6 (S 3 ). The construction of e
is over B, so f = h ◦ e as actual maps. This proves [f ] = 0.
    For a second proof, let S1 , S2 be the reduced multiple fibres. The line bundles OX (Sj ) are
topologically trivial because H 2 (X; Z) = 0. The coordinate sections of f ∗ O(1) have divisors
3S1 and 4S2 after a Mobius change of base coordinate. Choose a smooth frame of f ∗ O(1).

of OX (S1 ) and OX (S2 ) whose third and fourth powers, under the given divisor isomorphisms,

2.3   B.3. The four workbench maps
The exact maps, including their suspension conventions, are needed here. Put T = (Λ ⊗ R)/Λ
and let π : N0 \ W → T be the long-period quotient. On the punctured cusp write q = reiφ .

its lower vertex, and sends the complement of the cusp neighbourhood to its upper vertex.
Collapsing the two-skeleton of S 1 × T = T 3 and then taking the reduced suspension gives
H : X → S 4 . Collapsing the one-skeleton of T = T 2 and forgetting φ gives qb3 : X → S 3 .
Retaining only γ and forgetting φ gives qbγ : X → S 2 . These are the maps in the supplied
workbench, not choices of arbitrary sphere quotients of the same targets.

2.5   B.5. A cell presentation from the three fillings
We give a topological cell construction, retaining the actual boundary maps before making

a smooth handle decomposition. Throughout this subsection p = −1, so the finite twists are
v1 = g + 2u − 4w and v2 = −g − 3u + 3w and the cusp gluing has zero translation drift.
    For a matrix A on F = R4 /Λ, our mapping-torus convention is

The positive interval loop ρ satisfies ρtλ ρ−1 = tAλ . This fixes the inverse in (B.5.1) and agrees
with the clockwise meridians used in A.1.

    Let A be the nonnegative real part of the frozen toric cover over |q| ≤ η, and A0 its
central part. The local orthant descriptions make A a three-manifold with boundary; the
corners may be rounded. Its interior has coordinates (y, ρ) ∈ R2 × (0, η), y = log |x|/ log ρ.
The positive period action is y 7→ y + Bρ+ λ, where Bρ+ = B0 − 2π Im C0 / log ρ. For small
η these matrices are invertible. Thus the interior of the positive quotient Q+ is explicitly
T 2 × (0, η), using a = (Bρ+ )−1 y. The bounded fundamental parallelogram meets only finitely
many of the toric bounded-position charts, including at ρ = 0, so Q+ is compact. Its two
boundary components are tori. The inner one is the honeycomb quotient, and the outer one
is the positive regular-fibre torus.
    Both boundary inclusions induce the identity on the period deck group Z2 . Indeed A0
is the honeycomb plane and hence contractible; A is contractible because its interior is
contractible and pushing a boundary collar inward gives a homotopy equivalence with that
interior. The quotient is irreducible. An embedded locally flat two-sphere lies in its interior
T 2 × (0, η). Lift it to R2 × R. Its bounded ball is disjoint from all its nonzero lattice translates:
disjoint boundary spheres would otherwise give nested balls, impossible for translates of equal
finite volume. The ball therefore descends. This also proves irreducibility of the product
target T 2 × I. The boundary tori are incompressible because their fundamental groups inject.
    There is a map of pairs Q+ → T 2 × I inducing the identity on π1 and restricting to
the prescribed homeomorphisms on the two boundaries. For its first coordinate, extend the
classifying map to T 2 = K(Z2 , 1) and use the homotopy extension property on the boundary;
use a collar height for the second coordinate. Apply [Wal68, Theorem 6.1, p. 77] to this
map. The source is sufficiently large, since a boundary torus pushed into its interior is
incompressible. The product target has the same property, and all the other hypotheses were
just verified. The homotopy is fixed on the boundary. Its alternative of mapping the connected
source into the boundary is impossible, since the two source boundaries map to distinct
target components. It therefore ends at a covering map. The induced fundamental-group
isomorphism makes that covering one-sheeted. We obtain a product homeomorphism relative
to both prescribed boundary markings.
    Lift this product to A and spread it by compact phases. The full period action on a phase
(φ, ϑ) is (φ, ϑ) 7→ (uλ φϑB0 λ , ϑ); it does not depend on the positive radial point. The lifted
product is therefore equivariant for the full action. Phase stabilizers occur only on A0 and
are exactly those of (B.5.4). Consequently the resulting quotient is the mapping cylinder of
the boundary phase map. On the component with centre v, the q-phase acts on Tf by −v
times that phase, since (v, 1) is the stabilizer ray. Substituting the clockwise interval phase
and the marked period −θB0 a gives precisely (B.5.6).

2.6   B.6. Smooth monodromy: every requested class is zero
This subsection settles B.6 for the original family and every sphere-producing higher-
multiplicity family of K1. We use the complex orientation of X, the positive loop in
the w-plane, and the generator of Θ7 with Eells–Kuiper invariant 1/28, as in the conventions
and the supplied result K3. Write a = [Φ] ∈ Z/28. The mapping torus has the oriented
diffeomorphism type (S 1 × S 6 )#ΣΦ . The reduction from this mapping torus to the glued
sphere, and the independence of its Eells–Kuiper invariant from the two spin structures, are
those of K3; no different convention is introduced here.

Proposition B.6.1 (Proved; precise scope of K7). If the monodromy of the sixfold
parameter pullback has computed class b = 6a ∈ Z/28, then b is even and, writing b = 2r,
the original class satisfies
                                 a ≡ 5r (mod 14).
There are exactly two residues modulo 28 satisfying this condition, and they differ by 14.
Without a value of b, this assertion excludes none of the 28 possibilities for a.

Proof. Pulling a mapping torus back by a degree-six map of its oriented base circle replaces
its monodromy by Φ6 . Thus its class is 6a. The kernel of multiplication by six on Z/28 is
{0, 14} and its image consists of the even residues. Dividing 6a = 2r by two gives 3a = r
modulo 14; multiplication by five inverts three modulo 14. Every a has an image under
this multiplication, so the conditional statement does not itself restrict a. This is the exact
arithmetic content of K7, not a computation of the sixfold monodromy.

Theorem B.6.2 (Proved: complete answer to B.6). The original class is a = 0,
and the corresponding class for every sphere-producing family X3k,4l is also zero for the
positive loop with period 2kl. The original computation is B.6.21; the actual higher-family
replacement and cup calculation are B.6.22–B.6.23, and the complete spin-trace comparison
proving the assertion is B.6.24. Corollary B.6.25 then gives an explicit spin filling of every
resulting mapping torus, with one zero-handle and one one-handle. Propositions B.6.3–B.6.6
give a separate analytic conifold reduction for every pair; they do not by themselves evaluate
or compare the numerical classes. The following records retain the earlier unsuccessful
parameter-filling approaches, followed by the completed smooth calculation for all requested
pairs.

Proof. We first construct the surgery trace around the whole parameter circle, including its
gluing. The even-shift comparisons in B.6.3 preserve the actual smoothing parameter s, not

The relative holomorphic Morse coordinates consequently have transition germs preserving

Such a germ F retracts to its derivative by Fr (z) = r−1 F (rz), 0 < r ≤ 1, with F0 = dF0 ; each
germ in this deformation still preserves the quadratic function. The chosen small resolution is
part of the family, so these derivatives preserve its ruling. They therefore belong to SO(4, C)
rather than the component which exchanges the two rulings. Reduce this group to its maximal
compact SO(4) and choose small invariant collars. The deformation of germs gives the same
boundary bundles up to isotopy, and collar isotopies extend to their adjacent pieces.

Proposition B.6.6 (Proved; the reduction for all coprime multiplicities). For every

remain undetermined here.

Proof. Put h = 2kl. The D.3 construction applies with the finite replacements of orders
3k, 4l: their affine actions are still free, and multiplying the linearization by 1 − st is a unit
change on each of their fixed root discs. The node and its small resolution are unchanged.
The one-surgery proof of D.3.2 therefore identifies the smoothing with S 3 × S 3 .
    We spell out why the comparison from K1 survives the separated cusps. Use the fixed-data
case of its proof, so the first coordinates of its rational finite translation vectors bj , integral
defects `j , and connector vectors dj are all zero. Changing β to β − Ls changes only the
b column of the period matrix. It consequently leaves these finite translation formulas
γ
unchanged. In K1 the remaining cusp defect has already been adjusted to belong to Zw ⊕ Zd;
write it as aw + bd. Assign aw to the old elliptic node and bd to the new δ node. Their
product is the old defect, since Cw d = d. Each is an allowed integral winding in its primitive
rank-one toric direction. Realize it locally by the appropriate integer power of the base
coordinate, times a holomorphic unit; the transverse elliptic translation is holomorphic. These
are precisely the extending rank-one translations and they agree with the unsplit two-direction
prescription when the two zeros coincide.
    The differences of these local prescriptions have the same coarse vertical-vector sheaf as
in K1:
                              0 −→ OB −→ VB −→ OB (−p0 ) −→ 0.
To check this assertion locally, quotient by the invariant δ vector. The quotient is the Lie
line of the unchanged elliptic surface; its finite-root exponents and its simple pole at the
old elliptic node are unchanged. The new δ-direction node has a nonvanishing logarithmic
δ generator in the abstract vertical bundle and a regular transverse elliptic generator, so it
adds no zero or pole to that quotient. The extra subgroups in the enlarged finite roots act
trivially on vector coefficients, just as in K1. Both end terms have zero H 1 , hence the Cech
correction glues the new local prescriptions. On a small parameter disc ∆s , including the
coalescence, this is the relative exact sequence

                      0 −→ pr∗B OB −→ VB×∆s −→ pr∗B OB (−p0 ) −→ 0.

The local logarithmic generators described above also define this sequence at s = 0. The
two-chart Cech complex for either end term has zero first cohomology, so R1 pr∆s ∗ VB×∆s = 0.
The same holds after adjoining a small Stein c-disc. Solving that relative complex supplies a
correction holomorphic in c, s, through the coalescence. The integral windings are constant
and the local units vary holomorphically; at the coalescence their two toric directions are the
original ones. The comparison thus covers the identity on s and on B, with the chosen small
resolution. Different corrections differ by the connected vertical translation group, so they
have the same smooth monodromy class.
    The four homological matrices are still (B.6.2). Finite transfer still gives (B.6.3), since
the root actions are free even when their multiplicity exceeds the linear order. Replacing

rank-two parabolic group proves the integral Torelli assertion.

zero. The same saturated-vertical tangent sequence proves p1 = 0 integrally, and the Kreck
sequence places the smoothing class in the central Θ7 . Finally the fixed-s trace argument of
B.6.5 applies unchanged and identifies this class with that of the original sphere family.

Proposition B.6.7 (Refuted; the scalar-shear claim already fails on the ordinary
locus). The first isotopy assertion of Lead 8 is false for the marked return of the original
family. On X ◦ = f −1 (B ◦ ), that return is not homotopic over B ◦ to

                                          x 7−→ ρ(−2θ(x))x

for a globally defined monodromy-invariant γ coordinate θ : X ◦ → R/Z. In fact, after
allowing arbitrary additional circle-valued scalar gauges on the base, a quotient of the affine
defect has exact order six. Its vanishing under the sixth iterate does not compute the sixth
iterate in Θ7 .

Proof. Take a compact pair-of-pants core P ⊂ B ◦ and the marked zero section on its ordinary
torus bundle. A connection for the compact family may be chosen to equal the flat real
period connection over this core and then extended over the three collars. Consequently its
induced return on the core fundamental group is the one calculated from the closing map in
K8. With base generators a1 , a2 and fibre translations tλ , that group and its return are

               π1 (f −1 (P )) = Λ o F (a1 , a2 ),        Φ∗ tλ = tSλ ,    Φ∗ aj = tdj aj ,

where S = I −2E and d1 , d2 are exactly (B.6.6). Different choices of the path from a basepoint
to its image conjugate this homomorphism by an integral fibre translation.
    The pure scalar shear has the same linear part S. For the zero-section coordinate its
two affine defects are zero. Changing the coordinate by a map P → S 1 adds defects in Zd;
allowing arbitrary such defects only weakens the proposed comparison. A homotopy over
P tracks the basepoint inside its fibre. It would therefore require, after quotienting by the
invariant Zd, an integral vector λ̄ ∈ Λ̄ := Λ/Zd with

                                   (Āj − I)λ̄ = d¯j ,       j = 1, 2.                       (B.6.15)

The possible sign from the direction of basepoint conjugation has been absorbed into λ̄.
Writing λ̄ = (x, y, z) in the (g, u, w) basis, the nonzero equations are

     6x − y + z = 1,        −6x − y − 2z = −1,              −y − z = 0,      −6x + y − z = −1.

Their unique rational solution is

                                        (x, y, z) = (1/6, 0, 0).                             (B.6.16)

It is not integral, proving the stated obstruction.
    This is independent of the auxiliary ordinary marking. Changing the basepoint path
changes (d¯j ) by one simultaneous coboundary. Replacing the lifted base generators by trj aj

                                                    31
changes dj by (S − I)rj , which lies in Zd and disappears in the quotient. An integral linear
change of marking transports both the local system and the displayed class. Thus none of
these changes removes the nonzero class in H 1 (P, Λ̄).
    Moreover 6d¯j = (Āj − I)g, and (B.6.16) shows that no smaller positive multiple is a
coboundary. Its order is exactly six; the three nonzero Smith factors of the stacked quotient
coboundary matrix are 1, 1, 6. Since Sdj = dj , the defect of the rth iterate is rdj , so the
sixth iterate is the first one for which this particular obstruction vanishes. In the full lattice,
subtracting that integral coboundary gives

                      6d1 − (A1 − I)g = −4d,             6d2 − (A2 − I)g = 3d.             (B.6.17)

These are the two scalar windings seen in K8, with the inverse sign if one reverses its
comparison direction. They still have to be matched to the finite and cusp collars to compute
a diffeomorphism class of the compact sphere.
    The arithmetic also explains a distinction in terminology. For a shift h = 2r, a literal
shear −hθ with a global γ coordinate would require the base windings of θ to be 1/3, −1/4,
after solving the quotient equations. Those are not integers. A scalar gauge whose hth root
is not globally defined is a different map; the sixfold scalar representative in K8 is of that
latter kind. On a simply connected ordinary base chart the translation has an additive lift
and can be interpolated, which proves the local shear statement there. It does not give the
asserted isotopy over all of B ◦ . Every rank, Smith factor and rational solution used here is
checked in maps_ordinary_shear_obstruction.py.

    The minimal elliptic pullbacks form a smooth projective family as p varies away from
0, 1, ∞: the two good-reduction coordinate changes in B.6.10 work relatively, and the twelve
nodal fibres remain disjoint. Their period maps are holomorphic by [Gri68, Theorem (1.1)]. If
the period in the order-four summand were constant, monodromy would preserve its positive
line and its negative orthogonal line, hence lie in a compact unitary subgroup. If the order-two
period were constant, monodromy would preserve the positive two-plane and negative line,
again a compact subgroup. The computed hyperbolic commutators exclude both possibilities.
Each period domain has complex dimension one. For any fixed nonzero rational vector, being
of type (1, 1) is a proper period hyperplane condition, so its preimage in this nonconstant
one-dimensional family is discrete. On the universal cover take the countable union over
rational vectors and a countable set of marking charts. Its projection to the parameter curve
is countable. Outside that set, neither rational Φ2 nor rational Φ4 contains a nonzero (1, 1)
class.
    Now let p be outside this countable set. The Mordell–Weil lattice embeds equivariantly
into rational (1, 1) cohomology by the orthogonal projection away from the fibre and zero-
section classes; see [Shi90, Lemmas 8.1–8.3 and Theorem 8.9]. All fibres are irreducible, so

                                                  38
its height lattice is integral, even and torsion-free, with every nonzero vector having norm at
least two, by [Shi90, Theorems 8.6–8.7]. Since P has norm two, it is primitive. The invariant
second cohomology has rank three by B.6.10; the fibre and zero section account for two
dimensions and P for the third. Hence Lηp = ZP .
    The only eigenvalues of an operator of order twelve whose fourth power is one have orders
1, 2, 4. The last two are absent from Lp ⊗ Q, by the period argument. Consequently Lηp = ZP
                                                                                        4


as well. For any Q ∈ Lp , write

                                      (1 + η 4 + η 8 )Q = mP.

Pairing with P gives 3hP, Qi = 2m. The integral height pairing forces m = 3r for an integer r.
Applying 1 + η + η 2 + η 3 now gives N Q = 12rP . Conversely N (P ) = 12P , proving (B.6.19).
In particular 6P is not a norm but twice it is.
    Finally any elliptic-surface automorphism covering the base deck generator is tQ η or
tQ [−1]η: its value on the zero section gives Q, and the remaining automorphism fixes zero
and is ±1 because the elliptic j-function is nonconstant. The twelfth power in the first case is
tN Q , which cannot be t±6P . In the second case the alternating norm has image in the η = −1
eigenspace of Lp ⊗ Q, which is zero. Torsion-freeness makes that norm zero integrally. This
proves the assertion about the sectioned conductor step. Replacing the elliptic surface by a
torsor removes the zero-section argument. B.6.13 constructs such torsor data, while B.6.14
isolates a further obstruction to using them as the requested filling.

Proposition B.6.13 (Proved; torsor and conductor-line data exist). For every
p∈/ {0, 1, ∞} there is a compact smooth holomorphic genus-one fibration π : Tp → Cp , locally
isomorphic over Cp to Sp , and an automorphism F covering η, with

                                            F 12 = t6P .                                   (B.6.21)

Its torsor class can be chosen to be annihilated by four. For p outside the countable exceptional
set in B.6.12 it has no global section. There is also a holomorphic line bundle M of relative
Picard class P such that, for the unique point cp ∈ Cp over p,

                                   M ⊗ F ∗ M −1 ≃ π ∗ OCp (cp ).                           (B.6.22)

Thus a linearization with a simple zero at that fibre exists. These are conductor data, not an
identification of a parameter filling with the prescribed mapping torus. The obstruction in
B.6.14 still applies to the direct one-component plumbing.

Proof. Let G = hηi ≃ Z/12, and let E be the abelian sheaf of holomorphic sections of the
identity Neron group of Sp → Cp in the analytic topology. Since all singular fibres are I1 ,
this is the smooth locus of the elliptic fibration. The analytic exponential sequence is

                                  0 −→ A −→ V −→ E −→ 0,                                   (B.6.23)

where V is the coherent Lie line and A = j∗ Λ is the constructible period lattice. This assertion
also holds at an I1 fibre. In the Tate chart the exponential is z 7→ e2πiz ; at the central C∗ fibre
its kernel is the invariant rank-one lattice. A local nonvanishing section has a holomorphic
logarithm near each value, proving local surjectivity.
    We first compute the obstruction group on the quotient orbifold B = [Cp /G], whose coarse
curve is B = P1 . Write q : B → B. The higher direct images Rj q∗ E, j > 0, are skyscraper
sheaves at the three branch values and are the cohomology of the corresponding stabilizers on
section germs. At such a point, choose a small invariant root disc. The formal subgroup at


                                                39
zero is uniquely divisible and its logarithm is a complex vector space, so its higher finite group
cohomology vanishes by averaging. Only the action on the central elliptic curve contributes.

Skyscraper sheaves have no higher cohomology. The coarse-map spectral sequence therefore

In particular the inflation of the cyclic class [6P ] vanishes in this group.
   The group–Cech double complex for G acting on E gives the five-term exact sequence,
whose relevant part is

                       H 1 (Cp , E)G −→ H 2 (G, H 0 (Cp , E)) −→ H 2 (B, E).             (B.6.25)

Here H 0 (Cp , E) = Lp , and cyclic group cohomology identifies the middle group with Lηp /N Lp .
Thus [6P ] is the transgression of an invariant analytic torsor class α. In Cech terms, invariance
supplies an isomorphism F of the torsor covering η; its twelfth power is translation by an
invariant section R, and the transgression is [R] modulo norms. Its sign is immaterial here
because [6P ] has order at most two. Replacing F by tQ F adds N Q to R and therefore
arranges (B.6.21) exactly.
    We justify the finite-order choice of α. The elliptic monodromy on Cp minus its twelve
nodal points contains both R1 and R2 : in the four-punctured downstairs group, multiply
either old loop by a power of the new-point loop to kill its covering character. The latter
has identity elliptic monodromy and covering character generating Z/12. Filling the ramified
points kills only loops with identity elliptic monodromy. The columns (1, −2)t of R1 − I and

annihilated by twelve. Replace α by 9α: its transgression is still [6P ], while 4(9α) = 0.

required holomorphic F . If this torsor had a section at a generic p, it would be the sectioned
model excluded by B.6.12, proving its nontriviality.

Proposition B.6.14 (Proved: the one-component torsor plumbing cannot fill the
required mapping torus). Let W → ∆r be a proper semistable family with smooth
complex four-dimensional total space, restricted to a small closed disc. Suppose that its
reduced central fibre is irreducible and that its normalization is a projective-line bundle,
or the stated conductor blow-up of such a bundle, over a genus-one torsor T → Cp with
Jacobian Sp from B.6.10. Suppose the map to B = P1 extends over W and restricts on that
normalization to the composite through T → Cp → B. Then H 2 (∂W ; Q) 6= 0. Consequently
this model does not fill the mapping torus of any finite iterate of either the sphere monodromy
or its S 3 × S 3 smoothing monodromy.
    More concretely, the proposed plumbing with conductor line OCp (cp ) and its simple zero
at cp produces a rank-one fibre of multiplicity twelve at p. A free quotient of this chart retains
that multiplicity. Thus the analytic torsor existence assertion does not by itself produce the
required primitive rank-one filling.

Proof. The small semistable total neighbourhood retracts to its central fibre, as in B.6.11.
Because that fibre is reduced and irreducible, its top homology is Z, generated by its
fundamental class; the normal-crossing locus has real codimension two and introduces no
further top-dimensional class. Therefore H6 (W ; Q) is generated by this central divisor.
Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies the map

                                 H 2 (W, ∂W ; Q) −→ H 2 (W ; Q)

with its divisor class. That class is zero: the central divisor is the reduced zero divisor of the
global parameter r. The exact sequence of the pair hence makes H 2 (W ; Q) → H 2 (∂W ; Q)
injective.
    We show that the extended base class is nonzero on W . The elliptic degree-one local
system on Cp has no global invariants. Indeed the cover is unramified above the original
I1 point and is a normal cyclic cover. Its monodromy group therefore contains the original
nodal transvection and all its conjugates, in particular its conjugate by the order-three elliptic
generator. The fixed line of the transvection is real and one-dimensional. An order-three
elliptic generator has no real invariant line, since its characteristic polynomial is T 2 + T + 1.
The two fixed lines are distinct, proving the claim.
    A genus-one torsor has the same rational degree-one local system as its Jacobian: local
translation changes act trivially on cohomology. The local smooth and nodal charts identify
its first direct image with the invariant extension of this system. In the Leray spectral
sequence of T → Cp , the only possible differential killing H 2 (Cp ; Q) consequently has zero
source H 0 (Cp , R1 ) = 0. It follows that

                            H 2 (Cp ; Q) −→ H 2 (T ; Q)   is injective.

Pullback from B to Cp multiplies the degree by twelve and is nonzero. Pullback to a
projective-line bundle is injective by the bundle formula. The conductor blow-up and its small
resolution preserve this injectivity: a degree-one proper modification has a cohomological
left inverse given by its oriented pushforward, or here directly by the unchanged conductor
section. Thus the class of OB (1) pulls back nontrivially to the normalization, and hence
nontrivially to W . Its nonzero restriction to ∂W proves the first assertion.
    For any diffeomorphism of S 6 or S 3 ×S 3 , the Wang sequence gives zero second cohomology
for its mapping torus, since both the first and second cohomology of the fibre vanish. This
remains true for every finite iterate. It contradicts the preceding necessary property of the
proposed filling.
    The local multiplicity makes the mismatch visible without cohomology. At the unique
point cp choose a coordinate z with t − p = z 12 . The proposed conductor section has a simple

                                               42
zero in z, so after multiplying coordinates by units its node chart is

                                             xy = rz.

For r 6= 0 this is smooth and the base map is

                                         t − p = (xy/r)12 .                             (B.T1)

The divisor over p is therefore twelve times each reduced local branch. An etale quotient
preserves the order of vanishing at a generic divisor point, so a free component-permuting
quotient does not turn (B.T1) into a primitive node. The required D.3 filling instead has base
function a unit times xy at a generic rank-one chart. This proves the precise local failure. It
does not exclude a model with additional central components, a suitably ramified total-space
quotient, or a different normalization. Those additional attachments would require their own
boundary comparison and characteristic-number calculation; blowing up only the central
fibre of the incorrect model leaves its boundary unchanged and is not such a comparison. The
exact root-chart and multiplicity checks are saved in fourfolds_B6_torsor_local.py.

It also gives H 4 (Q; Z) = Z and no torsion in these degrees. Integral duality proves the
assertion about y.
    We keep the complex structures on all torus fibres and on the local finite and nodal models.
On the interpolating annulus in B.6.16, the period matrix is smooth rather than holomorphic
in the base. It nevertheless defines a smooth vertical complex structure. An invariant
horizontal distribution extends it to an almost complex structure on the six-dimensional
fibres, making the map to B pseudoholomorphic wherever it is a submersion and agreeing
with the local complex structures near every critical fibre. Such horizontal choices form an
affine space off the critical collars, so they can be patched there and averaged over Sδ1 . They
are made on the parameter mapping torus itself. Thus they respect the actual closing map,
not just a chosen trivialization over an interval.

Ms → S 1 . The circle action on E is complex linear, and it is free on the base. It descends
to a complex bundle E on Q. The vector field δ and the parameter direction are invariant

In particular p1 (Q) = p1 (E).

     Let V denote the rank-two logarithmic vertical tangent bundle. It is the ordinary vertical

local extensions glue to the ordinary kernel off the critical loci. They descend to V on Q.

                                            c2 (V ) = 0.                                 (B.Q8)
    After division at the multiple fibres, the derivative has no remaining failure of surjectivity

                                 [E] = [V ] + [L] − [L|Z1 ] − [L|Z2 ].                         (B.Q9)
Here the last two terms mean the supported K-classes, extended by their complex-normal

The identity is consequently valid for the smooth interpolation as well: it is exact off the
critical curves, and on their neighbourhoods it is the displayed holomorphic Koszul calculation.
No integrability on the annulus is used.

Lemma C.1.2 (Proved; smoothness of a cover of the entire fan). Let Σ be the
complete periodic A2 triangulation at height one used for the cusp, in N 0 = Z2 ⊕ Z. Suppose
a finite connected holomorphic cover of its toric neighbourhood is etale over (C∗ )2 × ∆∗ and
has smooth total space. The cocharacter sublattice defining its restriction to this torus is
nN 0 for some n ≥ 1. In particular its intersection with the two-dimensional vanishing lattice
is nZ2 .

Proof. A connected finite cover of (C∗ )2 × ∆∗ is classified by a finite-index sublattice K ⊂ N 0 ,
since this space has fundamental group Z3 . The unique normal extension across the toric
boundary is the toric map with the same real cones and lattice K. This can be seen on

                                                    59
each affine chart by taking the integral closure of its monomial ring in the finite torus field
extension; the resulting monomials have exponents in the dual of K. The convergent analytic
version has the same local finite quotient charts. Uniqueness of normal extension glues these
charts and applies to the given finite cover.
      For a target ray rv = (v, 1) let av rv be its primitive generator in K. A smooth source
chart over a triangle with vertices v0 , v1 , v2 requires a0 r0 , a1 r1 , a2 r2 to be a basis of K. This
is the usual smoothness criterion, also obtained directly by identifying that chart’s semigroup
with the free monoid on its three dual basis vectors. In the adjacent triangle across the edge
(r1 , r2 ) the other vertex is r3 = r1 + r2 − r0 . Both target triples are integral bases. Equality
of their indices gives
                              [N 0 : K] = a0 a1 a2 = a3 a1 a2 ,    a 3 = a0 .
Expressing a3 r3 in the first source basis gives coefficients −1, a0 /a1 , a0 /a2 . These are integers.
Applying the same argument across the other two edges of the first triangle gives all the
reverse divisibilities. Thus a0 = a1 = a2 = n, and their three vectors generate K = nN 0 .
This already proves the result; connectivity of the triangles also shows directly that every ray
has ramification index n.
    The assertion is about the entire cusp fan. A cover can be smooth in one triangle and
singular in its neighbour, so testing one triple point cannot replace this argument.

Theorem C.1.3 (Proved; no smooth global Kummer extension). For N > 1, the
local map κN in Theorem C.1.1 cannot be the restriction, even to one component of the
inverse image of a cusp neighbourhood, of a finite holomorphic map Y → X from a connected
smooth compact complex manifold. Additional cusp sheets and additional vertical branch
fibres do not remove the obstruction. For N = 1 the displayed local map is the identity and
has the identity global extension.

Proof. Suppose such a finite map F : Y → X exists. Form the Stein factorization of the
proper map f F , with connected fibres g : Y → C 0 and finite map h : C 0 → B. Near the
specified cusp point, the fibres of g are tori and their maps to the corresponding fibres of
f are etale isogenies, with image lattice LN of (C.1.1). No component of the ramification
divisor of F can dominate C 0 : a proper dominating component would meet every nearby
regular fibre in this open set where F is etale. Thus all ramification is vertical. Delete its
finitely many base values, the branch values of h, and 0, 1, ∞. Over the remaining connected
base the map is a cover of torus bundles. On every sheet the image of a fibre fundamental
group is a finite-index sublattice of Λ, and continuation along a loop with monodromy A
carries it to ALN . Translations do not change this subgroup, since the fibre group is abelian.
    Follow a based meridian of the second finite fibre, choosing it to avoid the additional
deleted points, and then return to the same small punctured cusp disc. The resulting sheet
has image lattice A2 LN . It lies in some component of F −1 (N0 ); it need not be the original
component. Pull that component back to the unramified toric covering YΣ → N0 . This is still
a finite cover with smooth total space, etale off the central fibre. Each connected component
therefore satisfies Lemma C.1.2. Consequently its fibre image lattice must meet Vtor in a
scalar sublattice nVtor .
    The actual second monodromy gives

Theorem C.1.5 (Proved; normal singular globalizations). If a normal compact
complex source is allowed, the prescribed local Kummer cover does extend as one component
above the cusp, for every N . There is a connected finite flat such cover, branched only over
S1 ∪ S2 ∪ W , of degree

                 N 2 |GN |,     GN = h(A1 , −1), (A2 , 0)i ⊂ GL4 (Z/N ) × Z/N.               (C.1.4)

Here matrices and the second coordinates are reduced modulo N . The component in question
has degree N 3 over N0 and is precisely κN . For N > 1 other cusp components include
singularities; this is a cover by a normal space, not by a complex manifold.

Proof. Remove the three special fibres and write the result as X ∗ → B ∗ . The base retracts to
a graph. We choose a continuous section that agrees with the zero section of the marked torus
family on a cusp collar. Such a choice exists: the only obstruction is in H 2 (B ∗ , cusp collar; Λ),
which is zero since the based cusp loop is a free factor in the fundamental group of the
punctured sphere; equivalently, extend the given section along a relative graph retraction.
The resulting group presentation is

                π1 (X ∗ ) = Λ o F (a1 , a2 ),   a0 = (a1 a2 )−1 ,   aj λa−1
                                                                         j = Aj λ.

The restriction to the cusp collar is the specified splitting with monodromy M0 . A topological
finite covering of a complex manifold has a unique lifted holomorphic atlas, so it is enough
first to construct its subgroup.



                                                 61
   Map the free group to GN by the two generators in (C.1.4) and map the fibre lattice to
(Z/N )4 . This gives an epimorphism
                              π1 (X ∗ ) −→ KN = (Z/N )4 o GN ,
where only the matrix coordinate acts on the first factor. Let UN ⊂ (Z/N )4 be the subgroup
spanned by g, u, of order N 2 , and take the connected cover corresponding to the inverse
image of UN . Its degree is |KN |/|UN | = N 2 |GN |. An element λak0 of the cusp group lies in

and M0N ≡ I (mod N ) because (M0 − I)2 = 0. Consequently its cusp subgroup is exactly

    We construct the extension, including its normality and flatness. At any point of the
omitted divisor choose a polydisc with divisor z1 · · · zr = 0, 1 ≤ r ≤ 3. Each connected
component of the restricted finite cover is classified by a finite-index subgroup K ⊂ Zr . Write
M 0 = Hom(K, Z), containing Zr by restriction. Its completion is the normal toric analytic
space with ring generated by convergent monomials with exponents
                                           M 0 ∩ Rr≥0
over the remaining polydisc coordinates. This semigroup is saturated, so the ring is normal.
For each coset in M 0 /Zr choose its unique representative whose coordinates belong to [0, 1).
The corresponding monomials form a free basis over the original polydisc ring: subtracting
the representative leaves nonnegative integer coordinates, and distinct cosets cannot cancel.
Thus the extension is finite flat. It is also the integral closure in the finite covering’s local
sheaf of meromorphic functions; we do not use the field of global meromorphic functions on
the compact nonalgebraic space. Integral closure is unique, so these local extensions glue on
all overlaps, including the self-identifications of W .
    The resulting space is normal and connected; finiteness over compact X makes it compact.
The same uniqueness identifies the selected cusp completion with the already normal smooth
source in C.1.1. Theorem C.1.3 forces at least one other cusp component to be singular when
N > 1. This proves the distinction between the two source categories and the asserted degree.
Exact enumeration gives |G2 | = 48, |G3 | = 216, |G4 | = 3072; the accompanying program
checks these finite examples, while the construction proves the statement for arbitrary N .

    The local assertions in the supplied workbench are valid, with their two different degrees.
Non-invariance of its fibre sublattice alone does not prohibit a further base cover. The
entire-fan argument excludes smooth global sources; the finite quotient in C.1.5 gives the
different answer for normal singular sources with additional cusp sheets.

d, and 3x = `1 c, 4y = `2 c express the other two meridians as multiples of c. On the cusp
π1 (W ) = Λ, and the same map is surjective. Hence the inverse image is connected, with the
asserted lattice of deck periods. Since B0 (bu) = e1 and B0 (bγ ) = −e2 , its toric components are
indexed by Z2 /(Ze1 + dZe2 ).
    We compute the normalization resolution, retaining integral coefficients. Let R = Z[t]/(td −
1), where t moves one component in the e2 direction. The degree-zero row of the resolution
is the cellular cochain complex of the dual torus with this d-sheeted marking; its cohomology
is (Z, Z2 , Z) in degrees 0, 1, 2. The degree-four row is R in horizontal degree zero. In degree
two, write the six boundary curves on dP6 in cyclic order as

               E1 ,   H − E1 − E2 ,       E2 ,    H − E2 − E3 ,         E3 ,    H − E1 − E3 .

The restriction differential from the d normalizations to the 3d double curves, in the basis
(H, E1 , E2 , E3 ), is                             
                                   −1 −1 −1 −1
                         B(t) =  1      1   1    t  : R4 −→ R3 .
                                   −t −t −1 −t
Replacing the second row by its sum with the first and the third by its difference with t
times the first gives rows with sole entries t − 1 in columns four and three. The first-row
unit eliminates the remaining first-row entries. Thus this matrix is equivalent over R to a
matrix with diagonal entries 1, t − 1, t − 1 and one zero column. Multiplication by t − 1 on
R has kernel Z(1 + t + · · · + td−1 ) and cokernel Z. Therefore ker B is free abelian of rank
d + 2, and coker B ≃ Z2 . There can be no higher differential: all rows with odd vertical
degree are zero and the resolution has horizontal degrees only 0, 1, 2. The only extension in
degree two is an extension of free abelian groups, hence splits as an abelian group. This gives
cohomology ranks (1, 2, d + 3, 2, d) with no torsion. The universal coefficient theorem, applied
from the top degree downwards, gives the same assertion for homology. The normalization
resolution used here is exact on stalks: at a point with r local branches it is the augmented
cochain complex of the (r − 1)-simplex, and hence computes ordinary cohomology even at
the self-identifications and the triple points.

Proof. Let λ 6= 1 be a dth root of unity and let Lλ be the associated rank-one complex local
system on Xp . Its restriction to a regular fibre is nontrivial on γ
                                                                   b. The cellular cochain complex
of a torus with this local system is a Koszul complex containing the invertible scalar λ − 1
and is therefore contractible. On a reduced multiple fibre the finite torus cover has the same
property. Transfer, or averaging over the finite deck group in characteristic zero, shows that its
cohomology also vanishes. The regular region and all three boundary overlaps consequently
have zero cohomology with these coefficients, as follows either by their bundle spectral
sequences or by contraction of the fibre cochain complex. Mayer–Vietoris therefore identifies

and the degree-four row is one-dimensional. Thus this local system contributes one copy of C
in degrees two and four and nothing else. The trivial character contributes H ∗ (Xp ; C), which
is concentrated in degrees zero and six by [AC26, Theorem 7.22]. The decomposition of the
regular representation of Z/d into its characters computes the cohomology of the covering
and proves the claim.

Theorem D.1.7 (Proved: dependence of the smooth type and the count). Within
the multiplicity-(3, 4) construction, the oriented diffeomorphism type of Xp depends exactly
on d = |p|. For each d coprime to six it carries a punctured-disc family of pairwise non-
biholomorphic complex structures, parametrized by W = e−πi(c+k2 ) , 0 < |W | < 216. At
each fixed nonzero admissible linearization scale u = e−2πic it carries exactly two of these
biholomorphism classes. Its universal covers likewise have one oriented diffeomorphism type


                                                  67
for each d. This statement identifies dependence on the construction data. The complete
Zhubr classifying invariant and a canonical cyclic action are supplied in D.1.9–D.1.12.

Proof. We use the all-twist comparison R1, whose sufficient step is the integral norm equation
and analytic torsor gluing in S6_02, B.2.1. Specifically, equality of |p| and of W gives
p0 = ap, a = ±1, and c0 − c ≡ k2 − k20 (mod 2). The finite norm equations have integral
solutions; the remaining cusp defect is corrected in its entire rank-two quotient lattice, and
H 1 (O ⊕ O(−1)) = 0 glues the translations. The cusp map preserves the prescribed fan. These
are the steps that give actual biholomorphisms, including every discrete twist, rather than
equality of abstract numerical data.
     For fixed discrete data, varying c along any compact path in the admissible half-plane
gives a proper smooth family. Here the properness argument of S6_02 A.3.1 uses a bounded
correction C(t, c) in Z = sB0 + C: on a compact parameter path the effective logarithmic
lattice is uniformly close to B0 , so finitely many closed toric polydiscs provide compact
representatives. The finite free quotients and the ordinary torus parallelepipeds are uniform
as well. All charts are products with the parameter before their free identifications, so
projection is a submersion. The same proof does not use p = ±1, and therefore applies
to the present data. Integrating a horizontal vector field over the compact path gives an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of its end fibres.
     Given two data with the same d, first change one parameter by an integer to align its
value of c + k2 with that of the other discrete datum; use R1’s biholomorphism at this aligned
parameter, and connect the resulting parameter to the desired one inside the admissible
half-plane. This proves independence of every datum except d. Distinct d give nonisomorphic
fundamental groups. Every resulting diffeomorphism lifts to an oriented diffeomorphism of
universal covers; different d are distinguished upstairs by Euler characteristic 2d.
     R1 makes the map to W an exact biholomorphic classification. Since u = W 2 , its fibre at
fixed u 6= 0 is precisely the two points W and −W . No two of these are equal. The asserted
count and the punctured-disc family follow.

the path-loop Serre spectral sequence of K(Z, 3) the fibre is K(Z, 2) = CP ∞ . If t has degree
two, its transgression is the degree-three generator z. Multiplicativity gives d3 (t2 ) = 2tz
and d3 (t3 ) = 3t2 z. Since two and three are units and the total path space is contractible,
induction in total degree forces the base cohomology through degree seven to be the exterior
algebra on z: there is no surviving fibre class that could kill an additional base class in
degrees four through seven. Also z 2 = 0 because z is odd and two is a unit. This proves
exactly the low-degree base calculation needed below.
   The coefficient extension 0 → Z − → Z → Z/d → 0 gives the fibration
                                      d


                              K(Z, 2) −→ K(Z/d, 2) −→ K(Z, 3)

                                                   70
with transgression d3 (t) = dz. Its cohomology through degree seven is therefore computed
by R[t] ⊗ Λ(z) with this differential. The groups in degrees three, five and seven are R/(d),
R/(2d) and R/(3d), all Z/d, and the positive even groups through degree six vanish. There
is no higher differential in this range, by the base calculation. Universal coefficients, starting
in degree two, give
                            H2 = H4 = H6 = Z/d,         H3 = H5 = 0.
With coefficients Z/d the indicated transgressions vanish, and t, t2 , t3 survive; in particular the
cube evaluates as a generator of the dual of H6 . The same reasoning applies after localization
at every prime dividing d. At all other primes, K(Z/d, 2) is homologically trivial after
localization, as follows from its single nonzero homotopy group and the localized Hurewicz
theorem. This rules out additional two- or three-primary classes omitted by passing to R.
    Finally we use the product decomposition

                                K(A, 2) = (CP ∞ )r × K(Z/d, 2).

The first factor has torsion-free homology concentrated in even degrees, so  the integral
Kunneth formula has no Tor term here. Its degree-six free part has rank 3 ; tensoring its
                                                                         r+2

degree-four, degree-twoand degree-zero groups with the three cyclic groups just computed
gives respectively r+1
                     2 , r and one cyclic summands. The stated products evaluate on
these distinct summands, and each is a perfect detector in its coordinate. This proves the
lemma.

Theorem D.1.11 (Known, with derivation: the diffeomorphism type of every
cover). For each d ≥ 1 prime to six let Md denote the oriented simply connected spin
six-manifold with the following complete Zhubr data: A = Zd−1 ⊕ Z/d, b3 = 0, refined
Pontryagin class zero, integral cubic zero, and finite cyclic cubic as in D.1.9 in the basis
x0 , . . . , xd−2 , u. These data specify a unique oriented diffeomorphism type. One has
                                    ep ∼
                                    X  = M|p| ,        M1 = S 6 .

For d > 1 this is a classification by a complete published invariant; no assertion that Md is a
torsion-free connected sum is made.

Proof. We apply Zhubr’s Theorem 1 [Zhu75], with the definitions on pp. 794–795. Its invariant
quadruple consists of H2 , the middle Betti number, the refined class p and µ = f∗ [M ] ∈
H6 (K(H2 , 2); Z), modulo isomorphism. D.1.4 gives the first two data. D.1.8 gives p1 = 0
and the refined class satisfies 4p = PD(p1 ). Multiplication by four is injective on A, so
p = 0. D.1.6 and D.1.9 give precisely all the evaluations of µ enumerated in D.1.10. Thus the
entire quadruple is specified. Existence is supplied by the actual covers already constructed,
so its admissibility conditions require no separate realization assumption. The injective
classification in Zhubr’s theorem gives uniqueness and the displayed diffeomorphism. For
d = 1 the same data are those of S 6 . This also explains why integral cup products alone,
without D.1.9, would not have sufficed; compare the torsion discussion in [Rei24] before
Remark 4.7.

Proposition D.2.3 (Proved: Euler checks and parameter sensitivity). For any
of the semistable triangular rank-two Mumford fillings, its reduced central fibre has Euler
number twice the number of vertices in the dual torus triangulation. A rank-one wheel over
an elliptic curve, a smooth torus, and a free finite quotient of a torus have Euler number zero.
Consequently the total Euler number is the sum of these rank-two contributions whenever
all other fillings are of these types. The fibre configuration and multiplicities alone do not
specify the input topology: integer clutching must also be kept.

Proof. Inclusion–exclusion over the toric strata counts the zero-dimensional strata, since
every positive-dimensional complex torus has Euler number zero. These strata correspond
to triangles. A torus triangulation satisfies 3F = 2E and V − E + F = 0, hence F = 2V .
A rank-one wheel is stratified by bundles over elliptic curves, and each stratum has Euler


                                               73
number zero. A finite torus quotient has Euler number zero by multiplicativity of Euler
number for covers. The regular locus of the total fibration also has Euler number zero; Euler
additivity gives the claim. This is K15’s actual localization argument, applied to the present
cells.
    For the last assertion, even the finite computation needs the full rational vector, not its
class modulo the lattice. A smooth weight-zero log vector θ of denominator m has boundary
relation meridianm = fibremθ . Replacing θ by θ + v for an integral v changes that relation and
its marked cohomological boundary map. The executed semistable examples OS45,47,55,56
have π1 = Z for the zero clutch and trivial fundamental group for the recorded primitive
integer clutch, while the fibre multiplicity is one in both cases. These four exact comparisons
are saved individually in records/manifolds_explorer_runs/.

    The simply connected minimal smooth sector is classified in D.2.25–26 and D.2.35–39,

that H 3 of its central fibre is free of rank three. The normal tori are the sweeps of all three
integral invariant loops: the vanishing circle, whose rotation extends over xy = q, and the two
loops of the remaining elliptic factor. They are boundaries of relative three-chains obtained
from the section disc and those rotations or translations. The unit-factor deformation leaves
the marked boundary and section comparison unchanged up to isotopy. For the rank-two
filling, the same argument gives the two invariant angular loops and H 3 = Z2 . Thus these
are integral normal-torus classes; retaining only the vanishing loop in a rank-one piece would
omit two relations.

the generator is the image of (CP3 , CP3 ,→ K(Z, 2)) under reduction Z → Z/2 [Zhu75,

    The conic has normal bundle O(4) ⊕ O(2). As an oriented real rank-four bundle on S 2 it

sequence, with the attaching sphere representing twice the generator, gives H2 = H3 = Z/2
and all other reduced groups zero except H6 = Z. The mod-two hyperplane class extends
across the surgery trace, because it evaluates to zero on the conic. Bordism invariance
therefore gives cube one on Mconic . It remains to compute this cube on the entire family.
    Keep the common piece XD from D.2.7. The scalar involution ι(z, v) = (z, −v) has

the monomial coordinates (v, v 2 /z) have involution (−x, y), so both normal directions at E
have sign −1. At the other rank-one point, the induced translation of the elliptic factor is a
nonzero two-torsion point, with no fixed points. In a rank-two triangle the weights are two
odd normal weights and one even tangential weight. There is one vertical edge orbit and its
two endpoints are the two distinct triple points, giving the smooth curve C.
    The involution extends over the finite logarithmic quotient, and introduces no additional
fixed points there even when k is even. Indeed, an equality ιx = g j x on its central covering
torus would imply jn/(3k) = 0 in R/Z after applying ψ. Thus 3k | j, since n = ±1. The
equality would then assert that translation by e3 /2 fixes a point on a torus, which is impossible.
Away from the central torus the base rotation gives the same conclusion. This replaces the
odd-order shortcut in Wang’s order-three proof and establishes the fixed-set statement for
every k, r.

holds for every free affine choice of the two logarithmic fillings, even if the sufficient coprimality
condition above is dropped.

has fundamental group Z/3 and middle torsion Z/(3R).

Proof. Geometric data and the actual multiplicative fillings. The configurations and height
lattices are the primary Oguiso–Shioda/Fukae data verified in D.2.1. Each displayed pair
has height pairing one. At every fibre at least one of P, Q is locally narrow, and at each

                           row   Q on its higher multiplicative fibres
                            1    3 (mod 8)
                            2    5 (mod 7), 1 (mod 2)
                            3    3 (mod 7)
