Theorem F.2.7 (Proved: the orbifold quotient). For the specified torus fillings in
F.2, with affine multiplicities m1 , . . . , mk , the fundamental group of the total space has a
canonical surjection onto

                             hx1 , . . . , xk | xm
                                                 i = 1, x1 · · · xk = 1i.
                                                   i
                                                                                         (F.27)

Consequently a simply connected example with k = 2 requires gcd(m1 , m2 ) = 1. There is no
simply connected example with k = 3 and m1 , m2 , m3 ≥ 2. An affine multiplicity-one point
is an ordinary smooth point and reduces to the problem with one fewer multiple fibre.

Proof. Over the complement of small discs at the special values, the torus bundle projects
surjectively on fundamental groups to the punctured base. Quotient its fundamental group
by the normal closure of all regular-fibre loops. At a finite filling its root cover is a smooth
torus bundle over a disc, and its free deck group is cyclic of order mi . The covering exact
sequence shows that the quotient of the filling group by its fibre subgroup is precisely this
cyclic group. The boundary base meridian maps to its generator. Thus adjoining that filling
imposes exactly xm i = 1 after the fibre loops have been killed. At the index-one Kuhn cusp
                     i

the fundamental group is generated by the three deck loops of its dual torus; these are regular
fibre loops. Its base meridian contracts. Hence its filling imposes the ordinary meridian
relation and leaves no extra generator in this quotient. The base relation gives the product
relation in (F.27). Van Kampen proves that (F.27) is the resulting quotient, in particular the
asserted surjection.
    For two points, substitute x2 = x−1    1 ; the quotient is Z/ gcd(m1 , m2 ).       For three
points of orders at least two it is a nontrivial triangle group. One can see nontriviality
without assuming a classification of the total space. Take a geodesic triangle with angles
π/m1 , π/m2 , π/m3 in the sphere, Euclidean plane or hyperbolic plane according as their
sum is greater than, equal to or less than π. In the spherical case the possible orders are,

                                                245
after sorting, (2, 2, n), (2, 3, 3), (2, 3, 4), (2, 3, 5), and the corresponding spherical triangles
exist. The Euclidean and hyperbolic angle conditions give the other triangles directly. If
r1 , r2 , r3 are reflections in the opposite sides, the rotations r2 r3 , r3 r1 , r1 r2 have the stated
orders and product one. They therefore give a nontrivial representation of (F.27) into the
orientation-preserving isometry group. Its quotient cannot be trivial. Finally a free cyclic
action of order one is the identity construction on a root disc of order one, hence an ordinary
torus bundle filling and not a multiple fibre.

Proposition F.2.15 (Proved: automatic local complex compatibility). Every simply
connected datum of F.2 with two finite affine fillings automatically has finite linear actions
commuting with real complex structures. This assertion concerns the individual finite actions
and does not produce simultaneous global periods.

Proof. Let mi be the order of the free cyclic affine action defining the ith filling. Its linear
order divides mi . By F.2.7 the integers m1 , m2 are coprime, so at least one of them is odd.
The corresponding linear determinant is one, because a finite real matrix of odd order cannot
have determinant minus one. The relation M1 M2 M0 = I and the unipotence of M0 imply
det M1 det M2 = 1, so both determinants are one.
    A finite-order real matrix is semisimple. Its nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs,
and its only possible real eigenvalues are 1 and −1. Determinant one says that the −1
eigenspace has even real dimension. Since the total dimension is six, the 1 eigenspace also
has even real dimension. Choose a complex structure on each of these real eigenspaces by
pairing a real basis. On each nonreal isotypical real summand, multiplication by i in its
complex eigenspace supplies a commuting complex structure. Their direct sum commutes
with Mi . The fixed eigenspace is nonzero because the affine action is free, as in F.1.4, so its
even dimension is at least two.
    Each chosen structure makes R6 /Z6 a complex torus and the given affine map holomorphic;
thus it supplies precisely the local complex-compatibility hypothesis used in the subsequent
reductions. For three genuine finite fillings F.2.7 has already excluded simple connectivity
without this argument.

Proposition F.2.8 (Proved: exclusion of an involutory finite part). A simply
connected datum with b2 = 0, k = 2 and the stated finite affine fillings has neither finite linear
monodromy of order one or two. Its unordered pair of finite linear orders must therefore
belong to
                 {(3, 4), (3, 5), (3, 8), (3, 10), (4, 5), (5, 6), (5, 8), (5, 12)}.       (F.28)
The affine multiplicities may still be larger than these linear orders.

Proof. An identity finite generator would make the product of the two finite matrices finite,
contrary to its nontrivial unipotent cusp. Suppose the cohomology generators are A, B with
A2 = I, where the other finite linear order is odd. It must be odd because the linear orders
divide the coprime affine multiplicities of Theorem F.2.7. Write U = AB; the cusp condition
gives (U − I)2 = 0. Multiplication of this identity on the left by A and on the right by B −1
gives
                                       BA + AB −1 = 2I.                                (F.29)
For v ∈ ker(B − I) we obtain (B + I)Av = 2v. As B has odd order, B + I is invertible,
so Av = v. Every B-fixed vector is therefore globally fixed. The finite free affine action
has a nonzero fixed linear subspace, and F.2.15 makes its real dimension even; it is at
least two. Consequently the global cohomology invariant rank is at least two. The Leray
argument of Theorem F.3.1 shows that b1 = b2 = 0 requires that rank to be exactly one,

                                                 246
a contradiction. Inverse or transpose monodromy conventions give the same identity and
fixed-space conclusion.
    Finally take the complete finite-order list (F.3), discard one and two, and keep its coprime
unordered pairs. The eight pairs in (F.28) are exactly the result of that finite enumeration.
This is only a necessary filter, not a classification of relative positions or affine twists.

Proposition F.2.9 (Proved: the only first-cohomology pattern for two points).
For a simply connected two-multiple-fibre datum with b2 = 0, the rational cohomology
system V has one invariant, no coinvariants, and fixed rank two at each finite generator. Its
quotient W = V /Qe by the invariant line has neither invariants nor coinvariants. If one finite
characteristic polynomial on W is (T − 1)Φd (T ) with deg Φd = 4, then W is irreducible over
Q.

Proof. Write a = dim V Γ , b = dim(V ∗ )Γ and fi for the finite fixed ranks. Theorem F.3.1
gives a = 1, vanishing first parabolic cohomology, and f1 + f2 = 4 + b. By F.2.15 each fi is
positive and even, so b is even. The maximal square-zero cusp has ker N = im N . Therefore
every globally fixed vector belongs to im N , whereas every globally fixed covector kills im N .
The global invariant and coinvariant spaces pair to zero.
    Restriction of a globally invariant covector to the fixed space of a finite generator is
injective: averaging that generator is the projection onto its fixed space, and the covector
is unchanged by averaging. Its restriction kills the a global invariants in that space. Hence
a+b ≤ fi for each i. If b ≥ 2 is even, the even ranks satisfy fi ≥ b+2, so 4+b = f1 +f2 ≥ 2b+4,
a contradiction. Thus b = 0 and f1 = f2 = 2.
    The quotient W has no invariant covectors, since its dual embeds into V ∗ . If it had a fixed
line, its preimage in V would be an extension of the trivial line by the trivial line. Every finite
generator on this two-dimensional space would be unipotent of finite order, hence identity.
This would give two invariants in V , a contradiction. Thus W also has no invariant vectors.
    If one finite characteristic polynomial is (T − 1)Φd (T ) with the second factor irreducible of
degree four, every proper nonzero rational submodule has dimension one or four. In dimension
one that generator acts as the identity. Since the product of the two finite generators is
unipotent, their induced one-dimensional characters are inverse; hence the other generator also
acts trivially. This would be an invariant line. In dimension four the one-dimensional quotient
is trivial by the same argument, giving a coinvariant. Both have just been excluded.

Theorem F.2.10 (Proved: exclusion of three further order pairs). No simply
connected datum with k = 2, b2 = 0, and finite linear orders (3, 5), (3, 8) or (3, 10) has the
required maximal square-zero cusp. Among such data, the remaining necessary unordered
linear order pairs are
                           {(3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 6), (5, 8), (5, 12)}.                   (F.30)
When one order is five, the other finite characteristic polynomial cannot be (T − 1)2 Φ4 (T )2
or (T − 1)2 Φ6 (T )2 .

Proof. Let the second order be d ∈ {5, 8, 10}. Proposition F.2.9 gives an irreducible rational
rank-five quotient W , with finite characteristic polynomials

                           (T − 1)(T 2 + T + 1)2 ,      (T − 1)Φd (T ).

Since the invariant line of V lies in im NV , the quotient cusp has Jordan type (2, 2, 1). All
three local conjugacy classes are self-dual. Their centralizer dimensions are respectively
9, 5, 13. For the last value, the conjugate partition is (3, 2), so the dimension is 32 + 22 ; the


                                               247
finite values are the sums of squares of their eigenvalue multiplicities. Consequently the
invariant-sheaf Euler formula applied to Hom(W, W ∗ ) gives

                       χ P1 , j∗ Hom(W, W ∗ ) = −25 + 9 + 5 + 13 = 2.               (F.31)
                                             

If W were not self-dual, irreducibility would make both HomΓ (W, W ∗ ) and HomΓ (W ∗ , W )
zero. These are the degree-zero group and the dual of the degree-two group in (F.31). The
Euler characteristic would then be nonpositive, a contradiction. Thus W has an invariant
nondegenerate rational bilinear form. Its symmetric part is nonzero, since an alternating
form cannot be nondegenerate in odd dimension; irreducibility then makes that symmetric
part nondegenerate. Both generators have determinant one.
    Over C use Spin5 ≃ Sp4 and its explicit degree-two representation on the primitive exterior
square. Choose finite semisimple lifts R, S of the two orthogonal generators, choosing one of
their signs so that RS is the unipotent lift of their unipotent product. The orthogonal Jordan
type (2, 2, 1) lifts to a rank-one transvection. This can be verified directly, as follows. For a
rank-two square-zero skew-adjoint operator on a five-dimensional quadratic space, its image
is a maximal isotropic plane, and its nonzero skew form on the dual plane determines one
orbit under the complex orthogonal group. A rank-one symplectic transvection in dimension
four maps, under the primitive exterior square, to precisely that orbit: its logarithm has two
length-two blocks and one trivial block. The exact exterior matrices checking these ranks
and square zero are included in fourfolds_order_pairs.py.
    The first lift has, up to a common sign, eigenvalues 1, 1, ζ3 , ζ3−1 . Indeed a symplectic
torus with eigenvalues x, x−1 , y, y −1 has primitive exterior eigenvalues 1, xy, x/y, y/x, (xy)−1 ;
substitution of the two equal primitive-third pairs gives the asserted list. In particular R has
a repeated eigenvalue. The lift S has order dividing 2d, so it has no eigenvalue of order three
or six. Nor can it have eigenvalue 1 or −1: a symplectic pair x = x−1 = ±1 would make two
of the nontrivial primitive exterior eigenvalues repeat, whereas Φd has four distinct roots.
Thus R−1 and S have coprime characteristic polynomials.
    We finish with an elementary consequence of the rank-one companion argument. Two
matrices with coprime characteristic polynomials whose difference has rank one are both
cyclic. To prove this, let u span the difference image. A common invariant subspace either
meets the image nontrivially, in which case the two induced quotient matrices agree, or
is killed by the difference, in which case their restrictions agree. Coprimality forces that
subspace to be respectively the whole space or zero. The span of the iterates of u under
either matrix is stable under both and is nonzero; it is therefore the whole space, proving
cyclicity. Apply this to R−1 , S, since R−1 − S = R−1 (I − RS) has rank one. But a finite
semisimple matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is not cyclic. This contradicts the displayed
spectrum of R, and excludes all three order pairs. The same proof gives the final assertion:
replace the two primitive-third pairs on W by two primitive-fourth or primitive-sixth pairs.
The local centralizer dimension is still nine, so the Hom Euler characteristic is again two.
The spin lift has, up to sign, eigenvalues 1, 1, ζj , ζj−1 for j = 4 or 6. The other lift has order
dividing ten and has no eigenvalue 1 or −1 because its primitive exterior spectrum is simple.
Their spectra are disjoint, and cyclicity gives the same contradiction.

    We first prove that changing the lattice cannot remove the obstruction at the prime
three. Write R = Z3 and K = Q3 . The standard quotient lattice WR defined by A5 , B5
has irreducible reduction modulo three. Indeed Φ5 is irreducible over F3 , since three has
order four modulo five. Every proper nonzero A5 -stable subspace therefore has dimension
one or four. On a one-dimensional subrepresentation or quotient its A5 character is one; the
unipotent product forces the B5 character to be one too. The stacked and horizontal matrices
for A5 − I, B5 − I both have rank five modulo three, as certified in the code, ruling out those
two possibilities.
    This irreducible reduction makes WR the unique stable R-lattice up to homothety. To see
this, rescale another lattice into WR but not into 3WR . Its reduction is a nonzero invariant
subspace, hence all of WR /3WR . Nakayama’s lemma, or the elementary Smith form of the
inclusion, then makes it equal to WR .
    Normalize the quotient of any stable lattice in VK to be WR . Its intersection with the
invariant line is 3r Re for some integer r. The representation of the free group on the two
generators has extension class α ∈ H 1 (Γ, WR∗ ). This cohomology group is torsion free: the
coboundary map from WR∗ into two copies has full column rank modulo three, since WR∗ has
no invariants modulo three. The class α is primitive in this free R-module. Otherwise the
extension would split modulo three and V would have a trivial quotient there. The horizontal
matrix [A − I B − I] instead has Smith factors (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2), so it has full rank modulo
three.
    In a basis starting with 3r e, the extension class is 3−r α. Integrality is therefore possible
exactly when r ≤ 0. Changes of splitting introduce no further classes: the coboundary
image is primitive, so an integral coboundary over K is already an integral coboundary over
R. Thus these lattices are represented by multiplying the extension rows by 3−r . On the
quotient cusp NW has primitive rank-two image. The extra cusp map is the nonzero map
ker NW / im NW → Re. It is a unit for the displayed lattice, because its full cusp has Smith
factors (1, 1, 1); for the lattice indexed by r it is multiplied by 3−r . Hence the full cusp is
primitive exactly when r = 0. We have proved uniqueness of the primitive-cusp lattice over
R, without relying on a bounded lattice search.
    It remains to compute the obstruction on that lattice. We first justify the arbitrary-twist
comparison integrally. For any global invariant lattice take the primitive invariant homology
covector ` and quotient the van Kampen group by every fibre loop in ker `. The finite
presentations become [a, h] = [b, h] = 1, am1 = hr1 , bm2 = hr2 , where ri = `(vi ). The cusp
meridian gives ab = h−κ for an integer κ determined by its translation clutching (κ = 0
for the stated standard clutching). The cusp angular lattice lies in ker `, so it adds no
further relation to this quotient. In particular this is an abelian quotient with determinant
m1 m2 κ + m2 r1 + m1 r2 . Simple connectivity makes that determinant ±1. Reduction modulo
each mi proves both gcd(m1 , m2 ) = 1 and gcd(ri , mi ) = 1.
    The two finite fillings have free R-cohomology in the degrees needed here. In the
invariant marking whose first homology vector over R has `-value one, the map mi ` from

the reduced finite fibre to R/Z has connected fibre T 5 : the affine generator permutes its mi
preimage components by addition of ri modulo mi , transitively by the proved coprimality.
Its monodromy on vertical homology is Disi , where si ri ≡ 1 (mod mi ), possibly followed by a
translation. Thus it is a mapping torus of a power prime to the linear order. The translation
is isotopic to the identity and does not change its Wang maps. At the second point, over
R we may take the invariant first vector to be v2 /r2 ; its denominator is prime to three and
does not change the R-homology lattice. At the first point the covering degree m1 is prime
to three, so averaging and the transfer identify its R-cohomology withVthe invariant fibre
cohomology directly. In degrees one and two the matrices Di − I and 2 Di − I have only
unit Smith factors. This proves the stated freeness by the Wang sequence.
    The finite degree-two covering cokernel is read from integral periods. Vertical cycles have
integral periods. The remaining primitive two-cycle is the commuting torus formed by a base
suspension and a primitive fixed vertical loop λi ; its covering period is ω(ui , λi )/mi for an
invariant integral two-form ω. More explicitly the homological Wang sequence is

    0 −→ coker(Disi − I | H2 (T 5 ; R)) −→ H2 (Bi ; R) −→ ker(Disi − I | H1 (T 5 ; R)) −→ 0.

The last group has rank one, generated by λi . The commuting suspension torus maps to
that generator; at the second point the invariant vector v2 /r2 may be used after taking
R-linear combinations of integral cycles. Therefore vertical cycles and this one torus generate
H2 (Bi ; R), proving sufficiency of the period test. For integral bases of the invariant two-forms,
the numerator rows at the two points are

                                      (0, 0, 5),         (3, 1, 1).                         (F.35)

The vertical Wang quotient has no torsion, so those cycles generate the full free second
homology and the period test is sufficient as well as necessary.
    Since 3 | m2 , the already-proved coprimality gives 3 - m1 and makes r2 a unit in R.
Changing that unit twist or adding a fixed vertical vector does not change the three-primary
cokernel in (F.35): the former multiplies its generating period by a unit, and the latter has
zero wedge with the fixed vertical loop. The first finite point has zero covering cokernel over
R; the second has R/m2 R.
    The global invariant degree-two group is zero, and the degree-two global coboundary image
is primitive, with vanishing rational parabolic first cohomology. Therefore H 1 (P1 , R2 g∗ R) =
R/m2 R. The global degree-one coinvariants vanish over R, and there are no degree-two or
degree-three point-supported kernels: the finite cap groups just proved free, and the Kuhn
cusp has its sole kernel in degree four. The degree-three global invariant group also vanishes.
Consequently the only nonzero total-degree-three Leray term over R is E21,2 = R/m2 R; it has
no possible differential. Thus H 3 (g −1 (P1 ); R) = R/m2 R. The universal coefficient theorem
gives precisely (F.34).

Proof. By F.2.15 the finite actions are locally complex-compatible. By F.2.9, the rank-

the unipotent product forces the other value to be one. Thus W and W ∗ have no invariant
rational line of any character.

nonzero such form cannot have rank four, because its radical would  V2 be ∗a stable rational line
in W . It therefore has rank two and is a decomposable element of      W . If two independent
invariant rank-two forms existed, their sum would also have rank at most two; hence their
wedge product would be zero. Their two supporting planes in W ∗ would be distinct stable
planes meeting in a line. That stable rational line contradicts the preceding paragraph. This
proves the bound without an irreducibility assumption.

Proposition F.2.17 (Proved: an odd torsion obstruction in this lattice). For the
integral tuple (Av , Bv ) in (F.U6), any simply connected filling with free finite affine caps and
the fixed primitive Kuhn cusp has a subgroup

                                 Z/(v 2 − v + 1) ⊂ Tor H2 (M ; Z).                               (F.U9)

In particular, in this specified family of lattices only v = 0 and v = 1 can be three-connected,
regardless of the affine multiplicities and twists. The stronger exclusion for every stable
lattice in each rational class is proved in Theorem F.2.19 below.

Proof. First compute the global coinvariants in the hatted lattice. In the rank-five quotient,
the A0 relations identify f1 = f2 = f3 = f4 = t and qf0 = 5t. The number q = v 2 − v + 1 is
relatively prime to five, as its five residue values show. Thus these coinvariants are infinite
cyclic, with f0 = 5h and t = qh. The B 0 relations become qκj h, where

    (κ0 , . . . , κ4 ) = (2v 2 , v(v 3 + v − 1), v(v 3 + v + 1), −v 3 + v + 1, −v 3 − v − 1).   (F.U10)

Their gcd is one: it divides 2v by subtracting the second and third entries, and it divides
v 3 − v − 1 by the fourth; the latter is odd and is −1 modulo v. Hence the rank-five global
coinvariants are Z/q. The extension line is killed in rank-six coinvariants by (F.U5), since
(AbBb − I)(0, z)t = e. Consequently the hatted rank-six coinvariants are also Z/q. The lattice
change (F.U6) is an isomorphism over every Z(p) with p odd, so the odd part of the actual
rank-six global coinvariants is precisely Z/q.
     Let V be the degree-one fibre cohomology local system. The only difference between
R1 g∗ Z and j∗ V is a finite cokernel at finite caps; the cusp degree-one specialization is onto.
Thus
                              H 2 (P1 , R1 g∗ Z) = H 2 (P1 , j∗ V ) = VΓ ,
including its q-primary part just computed. The space of global degree-two invariants is zero:
the irreducible odd rank-five  quotient has no invariant

     It remains to check every possible source of the differential d2 : H 0 (P1 , R2 g∗ Z) →
H 2 (P1 , R1 g∗ Z). The cusp has no kernel in degree two. At a finite cap the kernel is torsion
in H 2 of that cap, namely torsion in its first homology. Simple connectivity of the total
filling forces the distinguished affine numerator to be prime to the actual affine multiplicity,
by the determinant argument of F.2.12. The cap is therefore a mapping torus of a torus
automorphism whose order divides the linear order, five or four. Its first-homology torsion is

supported only at the primes five or two, respectively: averaging over the finite order kills the

Theorem F.2.19 (Proved: a residual obstruction for every lattice). Let a rational
rank-six datum have finite linear orders five and four, a primitive maximal cusp on a stable
integral lattice, and invariant line L, with irreducible rank-five quotient W and no rational
global coinvariants. Suppose that at a prime p 6= 2, 5 the semisimplified reduction of a
stable lattice in W is the sum of the trivial module and an absolutely irreducible module
of dimension four. Then no stable integral lattice in that rational datum, with primitive
maximal cusp, and no free finite affine twists can give π1 = 1 and H2 = 0 simultaneously.
    For every v ∈ / {0, 1}, the rational family in F.2.16 satisfies this hypothesis at each prime
dividing v 2 − v + 1. Consequently the exclusion of those parameters holds for all stable
lattices and all twists, not just the lattice in (F.U6). The two remaining parameters are the
verified survivors of F.2.6 and F.2.18.

Proof. We first give the lattice-independent mechanism. For any stable lattice VZ , use its
primitive invariant line LZ and quotient lattice WZ . The semisimplified reduction of a rational
representation is independent of its stable lattice. One elementary way to see this is to
compare two commensurable lattices by their finite quotient T . The exact sequence obtained
by reduction modulo p has end terms T [p] and T /pT , which have the same composition


                                                 258
factors by the filtration of T by powers of p. Hence the two lattice reductions have equal
classes in the Grothendieck group of finite-length modules. Chaining such comparisons proves
the assertion for any two lattices.
    Thus WZ /pWZ has length two, with one trivial constituent and one irreducible four-
dimensional constituent. It has either a trivial submodule or a trivial quotient (and possibly
both).
    Suppose first that it has a trivial submodule. Its inverse image in VZ /pVZ is an extension of
a trivial module by a trivial module. Each finite generator acts on this two-dimensional space
by a unipotent matrix. Since its order is five or four, prime to p, it acts as the identity. There
are therefore at least two global invariant vectors in degree-one fibre cohomology modulo p.
Write their dimension as ap ≥ 2; this is also the dimension of the global coinvariants of fibre
homology over Fp , by the perfect pairing between fibre homology and cohomology.
    The abelianized van Kampen presentation now shows

                                       b1 (M ; Fp ) ≥ ap − 1.                              (F.U12)

Indeed, after the monodromy relations the fibre contributes ap dimensions, and the two finite
meridians contribute two more. The two finite power relations and the single base relation
impose at most three linear relations. The cusp introduces no further fibre relation in this
abelianization. On the dual homology lattice its nilpotent operator is still primitive and
maximal, so its angular lattice is ker(M0 − I) = im(M0 − I) by primitivity, and the latter
image already vanishes among the global monodromy relations. Its base meridian is the base
relation just counted. Changing affine twists changes coefficients of these three relations, not
their number. Thus (F.U12) contradicts simple connectivity.
    Suppose instead that the reduction of W has a trivial quotient. Its integral global
coinvariants have nonzero p-primary torsion, since they have rational rank zero. The natural
map from the global coinvariants of V to those of W is an isomorphism. To check its kernel,
a primitive generator e of LZ lies in ker(M0 − I) = im(M0 − I), and hence is already zero
among global coinvariants. Therefore H 2 (R1 ) has nonzero p-primary torsion. If the total
space were simply connected, the finite-cap argument of F.2.17 would make every possible
torsion source in H 0 (R2 ) supported only at two and five. The invariant part of 2 V is
                                                                                            V
zero by irreducibility of the odd-dimensional quotient. Consequently the nonzero p-primary
subgroup survives to H 3 (M ; Z) and then to Tor H2 (M ; Z), again a contradiction. This proves
the general criterion.
    For its application to F.2.16, let p | q = v 2 − v + 1. We have p 6= 2, 5. In the original cycle
lattice of (F.U1), Y 1 = 2q(−1, 1 − v)t , so 1 gives a trivial submodule after reduction. On
the four-dimensional quotient the first finite generator has characteristic polynomial Φ5 , and
C = B −1 has polynomial (x + 1)2 (x2 + 1). This quotient is absolutely irreducible. Here is a
characteristic-independent proof over Fp .
    A one-dimensional composition factor would make the eigenvalues of A and C equal,
because CA−1 is unipotent. An eigenvalue of order dividing both five and four must be
one, which is absent from Φ5 . If the quotient were reducible, its only remaining possible
composition-factor dimensions would be two and two. On each factor, the determinants of A
and C must agree and have orders dividing five and four, so both determinants are one. The
two C eigenvalue pairs must therefore be (−1, −1) and (i, −i) in some order. On the former
factor C = −I, since its order is prime to p. Then the unipotence of CA−1 = −A−1 would
force the eigenvalues of A to be −1, impossible for Φ5 . This proves absolute irreducibility
and establishes the required residual composition factors at every p | q. When v ∈     / {0, 1}, the
integer q is greater than one and has such a prime divisor. The criterion applies.

Corollary F.2.21 (Proved: all good-prime lattices are forced). For a (5, 4) datum
with π1 = 1 and H2 = 0, the rank-five quotient has absolutely irreducible reduction at every
prime p 6= 2, 5. At each such prime its stable Zp -lattice is unique up to homothety. The
same is true of the rank-six extension among lattices with primitive maximal cusp. Thus,
once a rational pair in F.2.20 admits one survivor, all remaining integral-lattice ambiguity
is supported at the primes two and five. This assertion supplies no finite bound on those
bad-prime lattices or on the rational parameters.

Proof. Work first over an algebraic closure of Fp . Both finite generators are semisimple
because p 6= 2, 5. A one-dimensional composition factor must be trivial: its A and C
eigenvalues agree by the unipotent product, and their orders divide five and four. There can
be at most one such factor, since the 1 eigenvalue of A occurs once. If it occurs, the remaining
four-dimensional module is absolutely irreducible by the spectral argument in F.2.19. The
only other possible reducible composition pattern is 2 + 3. On each factor, determinants of A
and C agree and have orders dividing five and four, hence are one. The two-dimensional C
eigenvalue pair is therefore (−1, −1) or (i, −i). The first would give C = −I on that factor,
contradicting the unipotence of CA−1 and the absence of −1 among the eigenvalues of A. In
the second case the three-dimensional factor has C eigenvalues 1, −1, −1, so C 2 = I there; it
has an A-fixed vector because the other factor has determinant one and cannot contain the
simple 1 eigenvalue of A.
    Here is the required elementary involutory identity in the present characteristic. Put
B = A−1 on this factor. From (CB − I)2 = 0 and C 2 = I one obtains

                                       BC + CB −1 = 2I.

For Bv = v this says (B +I)Cv = 2v. The operator B +I is invertible, since B 5 = I and p 6= 2,
so Cv = v. The resulting common fixed line contradicts simplicity of the three-dimensional
factor. We have proved that any reducible residual representation has exactly the constituents
1 and an absolutely irreducible four-dimensional module. Theorem F.2.19 excludes that
possibility for a survivor, proving absolute irreducibility at every indicated prime.
    Let R = Zp and Kp = Qp . For two stable quotient lattices, multiply one by a power of p
until it is contained in the other but not in its p-multiple. Its nonzero residual image must

                                               262
then be the whole quotient by absolute irreducibility. Nakayama’s lemma, or the Smith form
of the inclusion, makes the lattices equal. This proves quotient-lattice uniqueness.
    For completeness the extension-lattice comparison is also integral. Fix a primitive-cusp
lattice VR , with invariant line Re and quotient WR . The coboundary map

                                       WR∗ −→ WR∗ ⊕ WR∗

is primitive, because its reduction has trivial kernel. Thus its cokernel, the degree-one
cohomology of the free group on the two generators, is torsion free, and an integral coboundary
over Kp is already integral over R. The extension class α is primitive in this cokernel. Indeed,
divisibility by p would make the extra cusp map

                                    ker NW / im NW −→ Re

divisible by p, contrary to the three unit Smith factors of the full cusp. Here NW has primitive
image: it is the quotient of the primitive image of NV by Re ⊂ im NV .
    Normalize any other stable lattice by the already proved quotient homothety so that its
quotient is WR . Its invariant line is pr Re for some integer r. The extension class in that
basis is p−r α; primitivity makes it integral only when r ≤ 0. Primitivity of the coboundary
map eliminates any additional rational change of splitting. The extra cusp map is then
multiplied by p−r , so its Smith factor is a unit exactly when r = 0. The lattices coincide
after the common homothety. This proves the full assertion and retains the bad-prime and
rational-parameter problems explicitly.

Theorem F.2.22 (Proved: a terminating lattice algorithm for each rational pair).
Let (A, C) be any irreducible rational rank-five pair in one of the eight spectral cases of F.2.14,
with A5 = I, B = C −1 , and (AB − I)2 = 0 of rank two. There is an explicit terminating
algorithm which decides whether the pair preserves an integral lattice, and, if so, lists all
such lattices up to simultaneous integral conjugacy. It then lists all rank-six extensions with
the same finite orders and primitive maximal square-zero cusp, up to simultaneous integral
conjugacy. The bounds below depend on the input rational pair and are proved to lose no
lattice. They do not bound the rational parameter space or classify all affine twists and
resulting homology.

Proof. We give the algorithm and its termination proof. The fixed line of A has dimension
one. Choose a nonzero vector e on it and a nonzero fixed covector ϕ. Irreducibility implies
that the vectors ge, with g a word in A, C, span the whole rational space; the analogous
statement holds for the covectors ϕh. In fact words of length at most four suffice. The spans
of words of lengths at most j increase from dimension one; if one step does not increase the
span, it is invariant under both generators and hence already the whole space. There are
only four possible increases.
    Choose words g1 , . . . , g5 and h1 , . . . , h5 giving bases in this way, and put

                            P = I + A + · · · + A4 ,     Tij = gi P hj .                   (F.L1)

rational basis of Mat5 (Q). Each belongs to R = Z[A, C]. Let R0 be their integral span and
set
                           R#
                            0 = {X : tr(XT ) ∈ Z for all T ∈ R0 }.                  (F.L2)
The trace pairing on the full matrix algebra is nondegenerate, as is seen from the matrix units,
so this is another full rational lattice, computed by inverting the 25-by-25 Gram matrix.

reduces its index by a factor at least two. There can be at most blog2 dc such enlargements
starting from R0 , so a bound of 1 + blog2 dc tests after adjoining I is sufficient. Stabilization

introduced belongs to their ring. It is then an order, and Λ0 = RZ5 is an explicitly computed

    Use a basis of Λ0 from now on, so R ⊂ Mat5 (Z). Smith reduction gives an integer c ≥ 1
with

Theorem F.2.23 (Proved: complete lattice classes for the two family survivors).
For each of the two rational representations v = 0 and v = 1 of F.2.16, there are exactly two

twists and multiplicities as a separate problem.

one, the two lattice representatives are

                              Z5 ,    Λ∗ = 2Z5 + Z(1, 1, 1, 1, 1)t .                      (F.L9)

The latter has index 16. The generic prime-by-prime implementation of (F.L5) and an
independent bit-vector enumeration give exactly the same two Hermite forms.
    For Z5 , the extension group in (F.L6)–(F.L7) is Z and κ is a unit on its generator. For Λ∗ ,
that group is Z ⊕ Z/2, again with primitive κ. Hence there are exactly one and two primitive

                      r1 = 1 + 5a,      r2 = −1 + 4b,            a + b + κ = 0.           (F.T10)

same extension argument identifies the glued manifold with the original twists (u1 , −u2 ) and
zero cusp clutching. If p = 1, the identical calculation starts from (−u1 , u2 ).
    Finally simultaneous fibre inversion identifies these two sign choices by an orientation-
preserving diffeomorphism. It conjugates every affine translation to its negative. It extends
over the Kuhn cusp: the lattice involution (x, h) 7→ (−x, h) preserves its toric fan, since a
simplex given by a chain in a unit cube is taken to the chain with reversed coordinate order
in the opposite cube. It normalizes the cusp lattice action and therefore descends to its
quotient, while fixing the base parameter. The resulting toric map is holomorphic, and in
the regular real six-torus inversion has determinant (−1)6 = 1. All translation maps also
preserve orientation. Thus every datum in (F.T1) gives the stated oriented smooth type and
has H2 = H3 = 0, proving sufficiency as well as necessity.

Theorem F.2.27 (Proved: the entire remaining order-six locus is excluded). Every

Theorem F.2.28 (Proved: universal fundamental group and twist normalization).
In the remaining (5, 4) locus, fix the marked standard Kuhn cap and allow affine translation
clutching. Let Λ = Z6 be fibre homology and let ΛΓ be its global monodromy coinvariants.
Write ΛΓ = Zh ⊕ T , with T finite, and let ` be the primitive invariant covector detecting the
free factor. The following are complete reductions for any datum that could satisfy π1 = 1
and H2 = H3 = 0.
    The actual multiplicities must be (5, 4), and the local vertical fixed pairings must be
h1 = 5, h2 = 4, as in F.2.25. For any affine twists and clutching the fundamental group is
abelian. If its free presentation determinant is nonzero, its order is

                             |π1 | = |20κ + 4r1 + 5r2 | |T |,     ri = `(vi ).               (F.T11)

If that determinant is zero the group is infinite. In particular simple connectivity is equivalent
to
                               T = 0,      20κ + 4r1 + 5r2 = ±1.                          (F.T12)
Whenever these conditions and h1 = 5, h2 = 4 hold, every such twist choice is oriented
diffeomorphic to the normalized filling with twists (u1 , −u2 ) and zero cusp clutching, where
ui is any integral fixed vector with `(ui ) = 1. Thus each eligible integral linear datum has
exactly one normalized smooth filling to test for the remaining homology conditions; no
affine-twist enumeration remains.

Proof. The image of the fibre fundamental group is a normal abelian subgroup in the van
Kampen presentation. After quotienting by it, the two finite meridians satisfy a5 = b4 =
ab = 1. That quotient is trivial, because five and four are coprime. The entire fundamental
group is therefore equal to the image of the fibre group and is abelian. This argument does
not assume that the normal closure of cusp vanishing cycles already exhausts ker `.
    In abelianization the monodromy relations give ΛΓ . The primitive cusp angular lattice is
the image of its nilpotent operator, and this image is already zero among those monodromy
relations. The remaining presentation is

                 5a = v1 ,        4b = v2 ,      a + b + v0 = 0    in ΛΓ ⊕ Za ⊕ Zb,          (F.T13)

where `(v0 ) = κ fixes the sign convention. Use any Smith presentation of T and split the
free part Zh. The full relation matrix is block triangular, with the presentation of T as one
diagonal block and the three-by-three free matrix of determinant ±(20κ + 4r1 + 5r2 ) as the
other. Its determinant gives (F.T11); when the latter free matrix has rank less than three
the group has positive rank and is infinite. For determinant ±1, elimination of the three free
variables leaves precisely T , even if the twists have nonzero torsion components. This proves
the exact simple-connectivity criterion.

                                                   273
    We give the global twist comparison to make its scope precise. Under (F.T12), the finite
fixed covector image is one at each point, so choose integral fixed ui with `(ui ) = 1. The
primitive vertical fixed vector λi and invariant covector ϕi satisfy ϕi (λi ) = mi , by the assumed
maximal local pairings. Formula (F.S5) makes the finite norm onto Zλi . Consequently every
vertical numerator component si λi is removed by the explicit cap translation (F.T8), whose
boundary residue has `-coordinate zero.
    For the complementary pair of pants the full relative obstruction group for extending
boundary translation sections is H 2 (P, ∂P ; Λ) = ΛΓ . Now T = 0, so it is exactly Z detected
by `, not just a rational or free quotient. Prescribing the identity translation at the cusp
therefore allows all the vertical finite changes to extend over P . The same argument removes
the zero-` component of any cusp translation clutching. For determinant −1, write r1 = 1+5a,
r2 = −1 + 4b; then (F.T12) says a + b + κ = 0. The two integer changes of finite boundary
marking and the remaining cusp change thus also have zero total relative obstruction and
extend. This gives the normalized twists (u1 , −u2 ). For determinant 1 the same argument
gives their negatives. The orientation-preserving fibre inversion extending over the Kuhn
fan, proved in F.2.24, identifies the two choices. All maps used in the comparison are cap
translations or translations by smooth torus-bundle sections over P ; the prescribed cusp is
retained throughout. This proves the claimed complete twist normalization.

    At five, work over Z5 . Modulo five the norm is (D1 − I)4 and is nonzero. Choose q with
Norm5 q primitive. The five vectors q, D1 q, . . . , D14 q are independent modulo five: otherwise
the nilpotent Jordan block generated by q would have length less than five. They are therefore
a Z5 basis. Thus D1 is the regular five-cycle permutation locally.
    At four, work over Z2 . The norm is (D2 − I)3 modulo two and is nonzero. The vectors
q, D2 q, D22 q, D23 q similarly generate a primitive regular four-cycle submodule Q of rank four.
The quotient is rank one with D2 = −1, by the characteristic polynomial. For a lift z of its
generator, put a = (D2 + I)z ∈ Q. Since D24 = I,

                                    (D23 − D22 + D2 − I)a = 0.

On the regular four-cycle module the kernel of the displayed alternating norm is exactly
(D2 + I)Q, integrally. One can see this by writing its four coefficients; equivalently D2 + I
has three nonzero Smith factors, all one, and the indicated rational image. Subtracting a
suitable element of Q from z makes D2 z = −z. Consequently

          M1 ∼ 1 ⊕ perm5       over Z5 ,     M2 ∼ 1 ⊕ perm4 ⊕(−1) over Z2 .                  (F.HC5)

These local comparisons apply to cap cohomology, not just to abstract representation lattices.
Indeed the integral lattice of intertwiners is the kernel of an integer matrix and its tensor
with Zp is the lattice of local intertwiners. Approximate a local invertible intertwiner by an
integral one whose determinant is a p-adic unit. Keeping the ui summand fixed produces
an equivariant torus isogeny of degree prime to p, preserving the normalized translation
±ui /mi . The resulting cap and boundary coverings induce isomorphisms on Zp cohomology:
the vertical torus maps are cohomology isomorphisms over Zp , so the mapping-torus Wang
sequences give the assertion. At primes not dividing mi , transfer already makes finite-cover
pullback an isomorphism onto invariants.

boundary classes in (F.HC3) have order two, so reversal signs do not change the tests. The
implementation uses (F.HC2) directly and hence does not depend on this comparison for its
validity.

conjugacy of their linear tuples and oriented diffeomorphism of their fillings.
    There are no data with three genuine finite fillings. With two fillings their actual affine
orders are five and four. Order the order-five point first. The complete, unbounded parameter
set is the rational projective normal form of F.2.20 together with its exceptional rational
affine line. For each parameter, run the terminating order, conductor, stable-lattice, and
primitive-extension algorithm of F.2.22. Discard precisely the integral classes failing (F.HC1)
or one of (F.HC3). The classes retained by this procedure are exactly all surviving integral
linear tuples. For each retained class all simply connected affine twists are exactly the choices
satisfying (F.T12); their fillings are all oriented diffeomorphic to its normalized filling. If
ordered labels with the order-four point first are desired, interchange the finite labels and
recompute M0 = (M1 M2 )−1 .
    Every retained datum has

Proof. The exclusions F.2.7, F.2.14, F.2.25, and F.2.27 leave exactly the stated minimal orders
and rational quotient problem. The rational normal form is injective on conjugacy classes,
including the exceptional line. The finite interval and extension-coset enumeration in F.2.22
gives every integral class over each rational point, with all bounds proved for that input. No
distinct rational points can become integrally conjugate, since an integral conjugacy induces a
rational quotient conjugacy. Theorem F.2.28 and the necessary-and-sufficient criterion F.2.29
prove both directions of the retention rule and account for every affine twist. This is also an
exhaustive enumeration if desired: enumerate primitive projective integer triples with first
nonzero coordinate positive by increasing height, and enumerate reduced rational exceptional
parameters by increasing numerator and denominator height. Every finite stage has finitely
many inputs, each terminates by F.2.22, and every rational input occurs. No finite cutoff is
imposed or needed.
    Hurewicz makes the retained simply connected manifolds three-connected. The only
singular contribution to Euler number is the Kuhn cusp, whose value is six by E.1.3; torus
bundles and the free finite caps have Euler number zero. Integral Poincare duality and the
universal coefficient theorem then give (F.HC13), including torsion freeness.
    For the smooth classification, F.2.15 supplies a compatible complex structure at each finite
cap, and the cusp already has its complex model. Choose their common fibre orientation
to be the one induced by the cusp. Commuting complex structures at the finite caps
can be chosen in that component: their two-dimensional fixed real summands allow the
orientation to be reversed when necessary. The fibre of the bundle of orientation-compatible
complex structures retracts to CP3 . Its connectedness and simple connectivity extend the
prescribed boundary structures across the two-dimensional pair of pants, exactly as in F.2.5.
A compatible horizontal distribution gives an almost complex structure on the total manifold.
Theorem F.1.2 therefore gives signature two, intersection lattice I3,1 , and c22 = 2. Since

H 2 = 0, p1 /2 = −c2 is primitive, characteristic, and has square two. The complete Wall–

and three-connectivity. It applies without alteration and gives the claimed exact oriented
diffeomorphism. Finally F.3.11 applies to the resulting determinant-one monodromy and
primitive cusp. It asserts the requested punctured-base periods with bounded correction, not
an additional unproved simultaneous good extension at all finite points.

    For the primitive Kuhn cap, the compact toric strata in its normalization and all their
intersection components are simply connected. Applying van Kampen successively to their
tubular neighborhoods identifies the fundamental group of the central fibre with that of its
dual three-torus. The nearby fibre map kills the angular lattice U and sends the long-period

relations, with no extra meridian relation left unspecified.

    Integral closure and two-point elimination. In a normal abelian fibre subgroup, the normal
closure of U is precisely the integer sum (F.G4). Start with its column Hermite basis and
repeatedly append its images under every Mi and Mi−1 , then take Hermite normal form
again. If the rational rank increases, it can do so at most three times. At the first nonincrease
the rational span is invariant under every generator and its inverse, hence never increases
again. If the current lattice has saturation index D in that span, every subsequent strict
enlargement divides this index by an integer at least two. There can therefore be at most
blog2 Dc such enlargements. This proves termination and gives the computable bound used
by the code; it never replaces a finite-index lattice by its saturation.

Proof. We first specify the complex construction and its marking. Over a small disc at the
ordinary value use a holomorphic period marking Tt = C3 /Λt . Let ωv (t) be the holomorphic
period vector corresponding to v. On the root disc t = sm quotient the pulled-back family by

                              (s, Z) 7−→ (ζm s, Z + ωv (sm )/m).                        (F.LT4)

Condition (F.LT1) makes v have exact order m in Z6 /mZ6 . Every nontrivial power therefore
acts freely, including over s = 0. The quotient is smooth, has a proper map to the disc, and
has central fibre of multiplicity m. On the punctured disc its holomorphic identification with
the original family is
                                                   log s

                              (s, Z) 7−→ sm , Z −        ωv (sm ) .                    (F.LT5)

Changing the branch of log s changes the second coordinate by a lattice period. Changing s
by ζm s changes its logarithm by 2πi/m and cancels the translation in (F.LT4). Thus (F.LT5)
is a well-defined holomorphic isomorphism of the quotient with the original torus family off
zero. Gluing on a fixed annulus supplies the asserted compact complex manifold: its charts
are the original charts and the free finite quotient charts (F.LT4), and it is the union of
compact pieces over closed base regions. The gluing is an isomorphism on collars, so the total
space is Hausdorff and smooth. The Euler number is unchanged, since the removed ordinary
torus cap, the new cap, and their boundary all have Euler number zero. This marking fixes
the new relation cm = v and zero extra cusp clutching.
    In the original datum the invariant normal closure of the cusp angular lattice is exactly
ker `, as proved in F.2.5. Adding the identity linear generator does not change that lattice.
The fibre image in van Kampen therefore reduces to the central generator h, while the original
two finite relations remain a5 = h, b4 = h−1 . The new relation is cm = h`(v) and the base
relation is abc = 1. This proves (F.LT2), including the absence of any dependence on the
vertical part of v.
    One may verify the Seifert identification directly: take a product circle bundle
on a three-holed sphere and attach its three solid tori with primitive meridian slopes
(5, −1), (4, 1), (m, −r). They are primitive by (F.LT1), and van Kampen gives exactly
(F.LT2). Its orbifold base has 1/5 + 1/4 + 1/m < 1 for every m ≥ 2. Pulling back the circle
fibration to its contractible hyperbolic orbifold cover gives a circle bundle on the plane, hence
the trivial circle bundle. The subsequent universal cover is the plane times R, and the fibre
subgroup is infinite cyclic. This also proves directly that none of these groups is trivial. The
rational Euler number in these conventions is r/m − 1/20.

Theorem F.2.33 (Proved: arbitrary finite affine caps). Let g(x) = M x + v/m be a
free cyclic affine action of actual order m ≥ 2 on T r , with M ∈ GL(r, Z) and v ∈ Zr . For

                     B = (D2 × T r )/h(s, x) 7→ (e2πi/m s, g(x))i,           Y = ∂B.               (F.CA1)

2r+1 . These are complexes of finite rank in each degree; only their indicated finite prefixes
are required to compute Hj (B), Hj (Y ) and Hj (B, Y ) for j ≤ d. Their maps retain the affine
translations and all integral higher coherence terms. In particular, the construction does not
replace an equivariant torus chain complex by its homology without recording the correction
terms.

     Scope of the chain result. The local finite pairs and the full cusp pair now have effective
marked chain models. To turn them into a universal integral homology calculation for arbitrary
nonsurviving F.2 data, one must also implement the maps from these boundary models to
the common torus-bundle complement, with its specified peripheral word and clutching
translation. The local results alone do not assert that this remaining global comparison has
been completed.

Theorem F.2.36 (Proved: simultaneous integral conjugacy for every input). There
is an unconditional exact algorithm which decides simultaneous GL6 (Z) conjugacy of any two
marked matrix tuples of F.2 and returns a conjugating matrix when one exists. The algorithm
does not impose a bound on their entries, on the affine multiplicities, or on the integral
conjugator. More generally it applies to any integral tuple containing a matrix 1 + N with
N 2 = 0 and rank N = 3; the primitive-image assumption is unnecessary for this statement.

Proof. We use column vectors and seek P satisfying P Xi = Yi P for every marked index,
including the cusp index. Put

                    H = {P ∈ Mat6 (Z) : P Xi = Yi P (∀i)},
                                                                                          (F.IC1)
                    O = {C ∈ Mat6 (Z) : CXi = Xi C (∀i)},            E = QO.

Both lattices are saturated integer kernels of explicitly displayed linear equations in thirty-six
unknowns. Thus Hermite or Smith reduction computes full bases, rather than sublattices of
finite index.
    We firstP decide rational isomorphism. For a basis h1 , . . . , hs of H, form the polynomial
f (c) = det( cj hj ). If it is zero, there is no rational isomorphism. Otherwise successively
substitute one of 0, 1, . . . , 6 for each variable while keeping the remaining polynomial nonzero.

                                                292
At each stage one of these seven values works, because the degree in that variable is at most
six. The final matrix D ∈ H is invertible over Q. This is a terminating exact test, including
the negative case, and not a search for a lucky invertible intertwiner.
    The full lattice L = D−1 H ⊂ E is a right O-module. Let J be the Jacobson radical of E,
let B = E/J, and use bars for images under the quotient map. We next verify the splitting
hypothesis needed for the principal-ideal algorithm. In a rational N -adapted basis,
                                                                   
                          0 I3                 A T
                    N=           ,    E⊆               : A, T ∈ Mat3 (Q) .            (F.IC2)
                          0 0                  0 A

Projection to A has square-zero kernel and image an algebra S ⊆ Mat3 (Q). A nilpotent ideal
is contained in the radical, so E/J ∼= S/J(S).
    Choose a composition series of the faithful S-module Q3 . The kernel of its action on the
associated graded module lowers this filtration and is therefore nilpotent. Conversely the
radical kills every simple factor. Thus this kernel is exactly J(S) and every simple factor of
S/J(S) acts nontrivially on a composition factor. For a simple algebra Matn (D), where D
has centre K and degree d over that centre, every nonzero simple module has Q-dimension
nd2 [K : Q]. If D were noncommutative this would be at least four, which is impossible in Q3 .
Consequently
                            B∼      Matnj (Kj ),                                      (F.IC3)
                                 Y
                              =                      nj [Kj : Q] ≤ 3.
                                 j

Every noncommutative factor is therefore Mat2 (Q) or Mat3 (Q); the remaining factors are
number fields of degree at most three. This proves hypothesis (H) of [BHJ22, Algorithm 8.3]
for every tuple under consideration.
     For clarity this decomposition is effective without a split-algebra oracle. Rational linear
algebra computes J as the radical of the regular trace pairing and computes the quotient
multiplication table. Its simple factors are obtained from its centre. A commutative factor
is a number field. In a noncommutative factor of dimension n2 , we enumerate integral
combinations e of a rational basis until the left ideal Be has dimension n. Such an e
exists because the factor is Matn (Q), so its rank-one matrices are rational points; clearing
denominators expresses one among the enumerated combinations. Left multiplication on Be
then supplies an explicit isomorphism to Matn (Q). The program verifies multiplication on
every pair of basis elements.
    The images O and L are a full order and a full right lattice in B. If the right order of
L differs from O, this lattice cannot be principal over that order. Otherwise Algorithm 8.3
of [BHJ22], in its right-ideal form, decides principality and returns a generator α when one
exists. The cited algorithm passes through a maximal order and its central conductor, tests
local freeness and principality over the maximal order, and solves the remaining reduced-
norm congruence in a finite quotient. Its correctness proof uses its Theorem 4.5(b) and
Theorem 7.9; its Theorem 8.4 specifies the number-field, finite-field and integer factorization
subproblems. These have unconditional exact algorithms. In the recorded implementation
the class and unit groups of every number-field component are certified with GRH=false
before the principal-ideal decision is used. The negative decision thus does not presume the
generalized Riemann hypothesis.
     If L is not principal, L cannot be principal. If it is principal, solve the integer linear
equations expressing α as a combination of the images of the chosen basis of L. This produces
a lift α ∈ L and an integral intertwiner P = Dα ∈ H. We claim that a simultaneous integral
conjugacy exists if and only if | det P | = 1.
    The sufficient direction is immediate. For the necessary direction, suppose P0 ∈ H is
unimodular. Every h ∈ H has P0−1 h ∈ O, so L = α0 O, where α0 = D−1 P0 . Write α = α0 u
with u ∈ O. Because both image elements generate L, u is a unit of O. Lift its inverse

                                              293
to v ∈ O. Then uv = 1 + j with j ∈ J ∩ O, and the finite geometric series for (1 + j)−1
shows that u−1 = v(1 + j)−1 ∈ O. Thus u is an integral unimodular matrix and P = P0 u
is unimodular. This also proves that any chosen lift of the image generator gives the same
yes-or-no answer. It is the right-module form of [BHJ22, Theorem 3.4 and Propositions
8.1–8.2], with the needed determinant condition written out.
    Every branch either proves nonexistence or returns a matrix whose integrality, determinant
and all intertwining equations are verified exactly. This completes the decision procedure.

    The implementation is code/fourfolds_integral_conjugacy.jl, with the pinned
runtime setup and runner in the same directory. It is an application of the published
lattice-isomorphism algorithm to the special centralizer forced by the cusp; we claim no
priority for integral-conjugacy decidability. The accompanying source-reading record identifies
the primary theorem statements and the precise implementation paths. This comparison
algorithm is distinct from a completed tabulation of all nonsurviving tuples or from an
arbitrary-height truncation of such a tabulation.
    The exact execution certificate has twelve comparisons. Six algebraic tests exercise the
full Mat3 (Q) quotient, Mat2 (Q) × Q, a rational multiplicity obstruction,
                                                                  √        a principal quotient
whose lift has determinant four, a nonprincipal ideal over Q( −5) with unconditionally
certified class number two, and a cubic centre with a certified rank-one unit group. Six
further comparisons use the actual admissible order-(5, 4) tuples with parameters 0, 1, 2: each
is recovered after an explicit large unimodular conjugation, and all three distinct pairs are
rejected. Their word traces tr(M1 M23 ) = 2, 1, −10 independently certify the latter negative
answers. All returned positive matrices satisfy every exact intertwining equation and have
determinant one.

Theorem F.2.37 (Proved: a complete canonical-representative algorithm). Every
marked linear tuple in F.2, for either k = 2 or k = 3, has a computable canonical integral
representative and a returned simultaneous unimodular conjugator. Two inputs have the
same representative if and only if they are simultaneously GL6 (Z) conjugate. The algorithm
uses a proved finite bound depending on the input. No fixed global entry bound can represent
every class.
    This is an effective classification, not a claim that its infinite output has been printed
in a finite table. The ordered involution sector has the separate complete finite normal
form F.2.38, and all of its 56 classes have been computed. The general bounded fallback is
potentially very expensive; its finiteness is a theorem, not a runtime estimate.

Proof. We first remove the existential condition about affine lifts from the admissibility test
for a linear tuple. A finite-order matrix M admits a free finite affine lift on T 6 if and only if
ker(M − 1) 6= 0. If this kernel is zero, 1 − M is a surjective endomorphism of the torus, so
every affine map with linear part M has a fixed point. Conversely let the order of M be d > 1
and choose a primitive u ∈ ker(M − 1) ∩ Z6 . The map x 7→ M x + u/d2 has actual order d2 :
its dth power is translation by u/d, of exact order d. For each prime p | d, the generator of its
order-p subgroup is translation by u/p, which has no fixed point. Every nontrivial stabilizer
contains a prime-order subgroup, so the whole cyclic action is free. If M = 1, translation by
a primitive half-vector is a free lift of order two. The invariant integral kernel is primitive, so
such a primitive vector is obtained by Smith reduction.
    Finite order is also effectively bounded at this linear stage. Its minimal polynomial is a
product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials, and eigenvalue one uses at least one of the six
dimensions. Every other cyclotomic factor therefore has degree at most five and their total
degree is at most five. For a cyclotomic index d, each prime divisor p has p − 1 ≤ 5, and



                                               294
its prime-power factors satisfy pa−1 (p − 1) ≤ 5. Enumerating these factors and the possible
degree sums gives exactly
                                 d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12}.                (F.CN1)
Here d is the order of the matrix, the least common multiple of its cyclotomic indices.
Multiplicities of a factor can only increase the dimension and introduce no new orders. Each
listed order occurs with a fixed vector after adding trivial summands. Thus taking the powers
in (F.CN1), checking the fixed kernel, the product relation, and the cusp Smith factors gives
an exact admissibility test. The unbounded actual affine multiplicities are not bounded by
(F.CN1).
     For an admissible full tuple T = (M1 , . . . , Mk , M0 ) let H(T ) be its maximum absolute
entry. If a three-point linear tuple has an identity at a finite position, temporarily delete that
identity, classify the remaining two-point tuple, and reinsert the identity at the same marked
position. There can be only one such identity, since otherwise a finite matrix would equal
the inverse of the nontrivial unipotent cusp. Deleting a fixed identity changes neither height
nor the lexicographic comparison of tuples in that conjugacy-invariant sector. This is only
a linear normalization: a nontrivial affine order at the identity-linear site is retained in the
gluing datum. In the two-involution sector use the canonical representative defined in F.2.38.
This sector is invariant under simultaneous conjugacy. In every other sector, order full integer
tuples first by H, then lexicographically by their row-major entries in the displayed marked
order. Define the canonical representative to be the first admissible tuple in the simultaneous
conjugacy class.
    To compute it, enumerate heights 1, . . . , H(T ) and the integer entries at that height.
There are at most
                                       (2H(T ) + 1)36(k+1)                               (F.CN2)
tuples in this complete box. The product relation allows M0 to be calculated from the first
k matrices, so the implementation enumerates fewer entries. It also rejects matrices with
different characteristic polynomials or orders before calling the conjugacy decision F.2.36.
These filters cannot reject an equivalent tuple. At least one comparison succeeds: the supplied
tuple itself belongs to its own box. The first successful comparison returns the canonical
representative and its exact conjugating matrix.
    Every simultaneous orbit has a least element in this order. Its height is at most the
height of any supplied member, which proves that (F.CN2) loses no class representative
for that input. If two inputs are equivalent they therefore return the same least element.
Conversely the returned conjugators show that equal representatives imply equivalent inputs.
The casewise involution normal form has the same property by F.2.38, and an involution
tuple cannot be equivalent to a tuple in the other branch. This proves the classification
assertion, including its finite stopping rule.
    Finally, F.2.16 already gives an unbounded admissible integral family. In its homology
convention direct symbolic multiplication gives

                               tr(M1 M23 ) = −v 4 + v 3 − v 2 + 2.                      (F.CN3)

This is unbounded even on the previously constructed free affine subfamily v ∈ 20Z. It
is invariant under simultaneous conjugacy. A fixed finite entry box contains only finitely
many tuples and hence only finitely many such traces; it cannot contain a representative of
every class. The input-dependent nature of (F.CN2) is therefore necessary for this particular
exhaustive procedure.

    The public implementation is code/fourfolds_tuple_classification.py. Its finite
involution branch has been run on all 56 representatives after nontrivial simultaneous integral


                                              295
conjugation, and returned every exact representative and conjugator. F.2.38 separately
records 112 normalization checks. The marked identity-insertion branch was also run on
all 168 conjugated inputs from the 56 classes and the three possible identity positions;
every representative and conjugator passed. The general height-box fallback has not been
exhaustively run on a noninvolution tuple; no such computation is claimed. Its underlying
exact comparison procedure was run on the twelve instances listed in F.2.36, including three
actual order-(5, 4) classes. The symbolic trace calculation is saved with its executable program
and output. The all-twist group algorithm is F.2.31, and the full necessary-and-sufficient
three-connected-survivor tests are F.2.30. These uses of the classifier do not presume that
arbitrarily many classes can be tabulated in finite time.
    When transporting a specified glued manifold, the returned matrix P also sends each affine
numerator to P vi , the clutch vector to P κ, and the supplied integral cusp marking to P Pcusp .
The multiplicities are unchanged. These are the actual linear changes of fibre coordinates
and therefore carry every boundary gluing map. The linear canonical representative does not
authorize discarding the cusp marking and independently choosing a different Smith marking
for the filled manifold.

Theorem F.2.39 (Proved: the full effective classification and all marked gluings).
The linear classification and all-twist topological computation asked for in F.2 have the
following complete effective answer. For k = 2 and k = 3, every admissible ordered integral
tuple has the canonical representative of F.2.37, with an explicit simultaneous unimodular
conjugator. Equality of these representatives is necessary and sufficient for simultaneous
integral conjugacy. There is no fixed global height cutoff; the finite stopping bound for
an input of height H is (2H + 1)36(k+1) candidates before the proved rejection filters. The
separate involution normal form has exactly 56 classes and is computed completely in F.2.38.
    For every choice of actual free affine orders and integer numerators, integral clutch vector,
and specified primitive Kuhn cusp marking, F.2.31 and F.2.35 compute the full fundamental
group and every integral homology group of the gluing. This is the fully marked correction
to F.2.3; peripheral matrices are not substituted for a choice of filling. The algorithms have
no cutoff on affine orders, twist entries or lattice indices. The complete list of data with
π1 = 1 and H2 = H3 = 0 is the constructive parametrization of F.2.30, with its exact lattice
enumeration and necessary-and-sufficient finite tests. Each retained filling has the homology
and oriented smooth type stated there.

Proof. The input is finite, so the prime-subgroup test in F.2.31 decides whether every
claimed affine cyclic action is free and has the stated actual order. The integral cusp test
and its adapted basis are F.2.1. The complete linear admissibility filter and the canonical
representative, including the proved finite stopping bound, are F.2.2 and F.2.36–38. The
characteristic-polynomial filters used by that algorithm are conjugacy invariants, so none can
remove a possible representative. The unbounded trace family (F.CN3) proves that no fixed
finite box could replace the input-dependent bound.
    We spell out how the linear classification is used with a specified gluing. If R is its
returned conjugator and P is the supplied cusp marking, change the data by

                   Mi0 = RMi R−1 ,        vi0 = Rvi ,     κ0 = Rκ,       P 0 = RP.            (F.SY1)

The actual orders are unchanged. The coordinate map x 7→ Rx on the torus intertwines the
finite quotient charts, since it sends Mi x + vi /mi to Mi0 x0 + vi0 /mi . At the cusp, its coordinates
in the marked Kuhn model are unchanged: (P 0 )−1 x0 = P −1 x. Hence it intertwines every
toric chart, translated face identification and collapse map of that fixed filling. It also carries


                                                 298
the clutch path to the path with vector κ0 . These maps agree on the collars and give a
diffeomorphism of the two fully marked gluings. Thus homology can be computed in the
original coordinates, while the canonical data and their group presentation are also returned.
Independently replacing P 0 by another Smith marking is not this comparison.
    An actual order-one site is ordinary, even if its integer numerator has been recorded. Delete
it by the explicit comparison of F.2.31: if it is the ith site, replace κ by κ + (Mi+1 · · · Mk )−1 vi
before deletion. The cusp matrix and its supplied marking are unchanged. There cannot
be an order-one site in an admissible two-point tuple: its other finite matrix would be the
inverse of a nontrivial unipotent matrix. Nor can a three-point tuple have two such sites.
Thus this reduction leaves precisely the genuine two- or three-point inputs of F.2.35 and loses
no case from the prompt.
    For each remaining input, the exact unsaturated normal closure, cyclic or triangle-group
extension and exceptional spherical Euler relation of F.2.31 give the full fundamental group.
The finite cap, complement and marked Kuhn chain maps of F.2.33–35 give a finite integer
Mayer–Vietoris cone through degree nine. Integer kernels and Smith reduction therefore give
all H0 , . . . , H8 with their complete torsion factors. This is a calculation for arbitrary supplied
twists, rather than a restriction to the affine orders of one displayed example. Its independent
abelianization check compares the resulting H1 with the van Kampen answer.
    Finally F.2.7–30 prove both directions of the survivor classification. Genuine three-point
orbifold quotients exclude simple connectivity. The two-point filters reduce every survivor to
the minimal order-(5, 4) spectrum; the rational normal form, finite stable-lattice and extension
algorithms include every integral representation above it. The universal affine normalization
includes every twist, and the six exact integral tests decide retention. Conversely every
retained datum satisfies all three topological conditions by those tests. F.2.30 computes
its common integral homology and applies the almost-complex and smooth-classification
arguments to identify its oriented type. There is no residual untested rational-height bound in
this parametrization. The canonical-representative algorithm can remove duplicates from it
if desired, but no finite global enumeration is asserted or needed for these complete per-input
decisions.

    The unified entry point is code/fourfolds_classify_gluing.py. It records the
original and transported markings, the exact linear normalizer, both group presentations
and the complete integer homology calculation. Its general noninvolution canonical branch
has the proved finite stopping rule of F.2.37 and the same stated practical limitation: that
astronomically large fallback is not claimed exhaustively executed. The executed finite
catalogue, conjugacy tests, full marked homology examples and their exact bounds are those
recorded in F.2.33–38. The identity-insertion branch has additionally been run on all 168
inputs obtained by placing an identity in each of the three marked positions of each of the 56
involution classes, after a nontrivial simultaneous conjugation. Every exact representative
and unimodular conjugator passes. The full unified driver has been run on the orientation-
reversing involution gluing of F.2.35 and on the same gluing presented with an additional
actual order-one site. In the latter test its numerator is (0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0)T and the original
clutch is (1, −1, 0, 1, 0, 0)T ; the suffix comparison reduces the clutch to zero. Both executions
return the complete canonical data, transported cusp marking, exact group and the full
integral homology of that example, with the independent abelianization check. Their outputs
and full JSON certificates are retained.

Theorem F.3.7 (Proved: compact holomorphic filling). The smooth eight-manifold
of Theorem F.2.6 carries an integrable complex structure. There is a proper holomorphic
map to P1 whose regular fibres are complex three-tori, whose two finite reduced fibres are the

fibre is the index-one Kuhn degeneration.

Proof. We first fix the dual convention. The preceding construction has cohomology

values are real. Choose a positive real basepoint and paths along the positive real circle
to infinity and to zero. Complex conjugation fixes these paths and reverses the respective
peripheral meridians. Pull back the preceding period family by conjugation of the base and
conjugate its complex fibres. Its Hodge subbundle is holomorphic, with local expression F(λ̄),
and its cohomology monodromies are A−1 , B −1 . Its homology monodromies are therefore
exactly At , B t . The third monodromy is fixed by the product relation, so this also fixes
its cusp marking. The primitive index-one condition and the bounded holomorphic cusp
correction are preserved, after replacing the real angular basis by its negative if necessary.
    For a holomorphic Hodge subbundle F with F ∩ F̄ = 0, restriction of integral homology
functionals embeds the homology lattice discretely in F ∗ . Real transversality makes its real
span the whole real vector space. The quotient F ∗ /VZ∗ is consequently a holomorphic family

of compact complex three-tori over U , with its zero section. This also proves local properness,
